UX_A11Y_CONT_005.title: WCAG Contrast (Minimum)
UX_A11Y_CONT_005.rule: Text and images of text must maintain at least 4.5:1 contrast against the background; large text at least 3:1.
UX_A11Y_CONT_005.detect: Automated contrast checkers (axe, WAVE, WebAIM) plus sampling computed styles on text over images/gradients.
UX_A11Y_CONT_005.when_to_apply: All meaningful text and images of text, including form labels and error copy.
UX_A11Y_CONT_005.when_not_to_apply: Decorative text, inactive/disabled components, incidental logotypes as allowed by WCAG.

UX_A11Y_FOCUS_011.title: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
UX_A11Y_FOCUS_011.rule: When a component receives keyboard focus, it must not be entirely hidden by author-created content.
UX_A11Y_FOCUS_011.detect: Tab through the page with sticky chrome present; fail if focused element is completely covered.
UX_A11Y_FOCUS_011.when_to_apply: All interactive components, especially with sticky UI chrome.
UX_A11Y_FOCUS_011.when_not_to_apply: User-opened content (e.g., modal) dismissible without advancing focus, per WCAG nuance.

UX_A11Y_TARG_004.title: WCAG 2.2 Target Size (Minimum)
UX_A11Y_TARG_004.rule: Pointer targets must be at least 24×24 CSS pixels, or satisfy the spacing exception with a 24 CSS-pixel diameter circle that does not intersect other targets.
UX_A11Y_TARG_004.detect: Measure CSS bounding boxes. If width or height < 24px, test whether a 24px-diameter circle centered on the box intersects any other target.
UX_A11Y_TARG_004.when_to_apply: All pointer-activated controls (mouse, touch, pen), including icon-only buttons.
UX_A11Y_TARG_004.when_not_to_apply: Inline text links constrained by line-height; unmodified user-agent controls; equivalent larger control available; essential/legal presentation exceptions per WCAG.

UX_ARC_FORM_010.title: Single-Column Form Layout
UX_ARC_FORM_010.rule: Present sequential form fields in a single primary vertical column rather than multi-column grids.
UX_ARC_FORM_010.detect: Layout audit: consecutive unrelated inputs share similar vertical positions outside allowed micro-groups.
UX_ARC_FORM_010.when_to_apply: Checkout, signup, lead forms, most consumer forms.
UX_ARC_FORM_010.when_not_to_apply: Expert dense enterprise forms with trained users; tightly coupled date/name parts.

UX_ARC_ISO_001.title: ISO 9241-110 Suitability for the Task
UX_ARC_ISO_001.rule: The dialog supports user goals without unnecessary effort or irrelevant complexity.
UX_ARC_ISO_001.detect: For a screen, mark elements not supporting the primary task; if a large share is irrelevant, fail.
UX_ARC_ISO_001.when_to_apply: Task-focused flows: forms, checkout, setup wizards.
UX_ARC_ISO_001.when_not_to_apply: Command centers / multi-goal dashboards where breadth is the task.

UX_COG_FOGG_013.title: Fogg Behavior Model (B=MAP)
UX_COG_FOGG_013.rule: A target behavior occurs when Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt converge at the same moment (B=MAP).
UX_COG_FOGG_013.detect: High exposure + low conversion: check if prompt is hidden, task is hard, or value is unclear.
UX_COG_FOGG_013.when_to_apply: Conversion CTAs, onboarding, notifications, habit loops.
UX_COG_FOGG_013.when_not_to_apply: Passive reading surfaces; automated backend processes; manipulative dark patterns.

UX_COG_HICK_002.title: Hick-Hyman Law
UX_COG_HICK_002.rule: Decision/reaction time increases roughly with the information entropy of the choice set (classically RT ≈ a + b·log2(n) for n equiprobable options).
UX_COG_HICK_002.detect: Count peer primary actions in a decision region; many equally weighted CTAs/menu items without grouping (often ≫7 visible peers) → overload risk.
UX_COG_HICK_002.when_to_apply: Nav menus, pricing tiers, settings panels, checkout decisions, onboarding choices.
UX_COG_HICK_002.when_not_to_apply: Expert analytic dashboards needing simultaneous density; highly learned expert UIs.

UX_DS_DENS_002.title: Standard Touch Target Size (44px)
UX_DS_DENS_002.rule: The default tap target size for elements relying on width and height dimensions on touch-enabled devices is 44px (2.75rem).
UX_DS_DENS_002.detect: Inspect the computed height and width of interactive elements (buttons, links, toggles) on touch devices. Flag elements where the clickable area is < 44px in either dimension.
UX_DS_DENS_002.when_to_apply: Designing buttons, list items, and interactive icons for touch-enabled interfaces (mobile, tablet, touch-screen laptops).
UX_DS_DENS_002.when_not_to_apply: Dense desktop-only interfaces operated exclusively by a precise pointer (mouse), where smaller targets (e.g., 32px or 24px) are acceptable.

UX_DS_TOKEN_001.title: Semantic Color Coding
UX_DS_TOKEN_001.rule: Color must be purposefully tied to specific meanings (e.g., red for critical errors, green for success, blue for tips/offers) rather than used for decoration.
UX_DS_TOKEN_001.detect: Implement linter rules restricting raw hex codes in UI components. Use visual regression or DOM inspection to check for non-standard colors or decorative colors applied to non-illustration elements.
UX_DS_TOKEN_001.when_to_apply: Designing alerts, badges, banners, buttons, and status indicators within an application interface.
UX_DS_TOKEN_001.when_not_to_apply: Illustrations, marketing assets, or brand-heavy landing pages outside the core functional UI.

UX_HCI_FITTS_001.title: Fitts's Law (Shannon Formulation)
UX_HCI_FITTS_001.rule: Movement time to a target increases with Index of Difficulty ID = log2(A/W + 1), where A is amplitude (distance) and W is target width; MT = a + b·ID.
UX_HCI_FITTS_001.detect: Estimate A from resting cursor/thumb zones and W of primary CTAs; flag frequent actions with high ID or targets below WCAG floor.
UX_HCI_FITTS_001.when_to_apply: CTA placement, toolbars, menus, drag targets on pointer UIs.
UX_HCI_FITTS_001.when_not_to_apply: Pure keyboard flows; voice; intentionally high-friction destructive controls.

UX_HCI_KLM_008.title: Keystroke-Level Model (KLM) Time Prediction
UX_HCI_KLM_008.rule: Task execution time can be estimated by summing the times of physical-motor operators (Keystroking, Pointing, Homing, Drawing), mental preparation (M), and system response (R).
UX_HCI_KLM_008.detect: Map out a frequent user task and sum the KLM operators. If the predicted time exceeds business requirements, the workflow is too complex and requires simplification.
UX_HCI_KLM_008.when_to_apply: Optimizing high-frequency, repetitive tasks in keyboard and mouse interfaces.
UX_HCI_KLM_008.when_not_to_apply: Touch interfaces (use TLM instead), highly exploratory tasks, or tasks dominated by complex problem-solving rather than interaction.

UX_HCI_STEER_011.title: Steering Law (Accot-Zhai)
UX_HCI_STEER_011.rule: The time required to navigate a constrained 2D path is proportional to the length of the path divided by its width. For a straight tunnel, T = a + b(A/W), where A is length and W is width.
UX_HCI_STEER_011.detect: Identify UI elements requiring continuous path navigation (e.g., nested hover menus). Measure the path length (A) and width (W). High A/W ratios indicate usability bottlenecks.
UX_HCI_STEER_011.when_to_apply: Designing hierarchical cascading menus, sliders, scrollbars, drag-and-drop interactions, and drawing tools.
UX_HCI_STEER_011.when_not_to_apply: Simple point-and-click tasks without path constraints (use Fitts's Law instead), or keyboard-only navigation.

UX_HFE_TLX_001.title: NASA TLX Multi-Dimensional Workload Assessment
UX_HFE_TLX_001.rule: Subjective workload is measured by deriving an overall score based on a weighted average of six subscales: Mental Demand, Physical Demand, Temporal Demand, Performance, Effort, and Frustration.
UX_HFE_TLX_001.detect: Review usability testing protocols. If subjective workload is measured using a single unweighted question (e.g., 'How hard was this task?'), it fails to capture the multidimensional nature of workload established by the NASA TLX standard.
UX_HFE_TLX_001.when_to_apply: Evaluating complex human-machine interfaces, aircraft cockpits, command and control (C3) workstations, supervisory/process control, and simulations where operator workload is a critical safety or performance factor.
UX_HFE_TLX_001.when_not_to_apply: Simple, low-stakes consumer applications where detailed workload breakdown is unnecessary; when purely objective performance measurement (e.g., time on task, error rate) is required without needing subjective perception.

UX_INX_CTRL_001.title: ISO 9241-110 Controllability
UX_INX_CTRL_001.rule: Users can initiate, pace, and reverse dialog actions; they retain control.
UX_INX_CTRL_001.detect: Find irreversible deletes without confirm; modals without dismiss; auto-advancing steps.
UX_INX_CTRL_001.when_to_apply: Destructive actions, multi-step flows, settings changes.
UX_INX_CTRL_001.when_not_to_apply: Security operations where undo would break integrity (document the exception).

UX_INX_ERR_009.title: Error Prevention and Fault Tolerance
UX_INX_ERR_009.rule: Errors should be prevented or easily corrected without serious consequences; preserve user input.
UX_INX_ERR_009.detect: Submit-only validation with page reload; cleared fields; color-only errors.
UX_INX_ERR_009.when_to_apply: Account, checkout, payment, and high-stakes forms.
UX_INX_ERR_009.when_not_to_apply: Validate-on-each-keystroke before the user finishes typing.

UX_INX_SELF_001.title: ISO 9241-110 Self-Descriptiveness
UX_INX_SELF_001.rule: The dialog is self-explanatory: status and options are clearly described without external docs.
UX_INX_SELF_001.detect: Audit controls for missing accessible names; placeholder-only fields; opaque errors.
UX_INX_SELF_001.when_not_to_apply: Universally conventional icons may use short names if the accessibility tree is complete.

UX_PRD_GUEST_001.title: Guest Checkout Prominence
UX_PRD_GUEST_001.rule: Guest checkout must be a primary, highly visible path; do not force account creation to purchase.
UX_PRD_GUEST_001.detect: Checkout entry audit: guest path missing, below fold, or weaker than login.
UX_PRD_GUEST_001.when_not_to_apply: B2B portals requiring authenticated purchasing by policy.

UX_VIS_GEST_006.title: Gestalt Principle of Proximity
UX_VIS_GEST_006.rule: Items close together are perceived as part of the same group, sharing functionality or traits. Proximity overpowers competing visual cues like color or shape.
UX_VIS_GEST_006.detect: Measure pixel distances between elements. If distance(A, B) < distance(B, C), users will assume A and B are more related than B and C. Check if this matches the logical data model.
UX_VIS_GEST_006.when_to_apply: Layout design, navigation menus, typography hierarchy, and grouping UI controls or form fields.
UX_VIS_GEST_006.when_not_to_apply: When elements are strictly independent, or when using other strong grouping methods like Common Region (borders/backgrounds) in highly space-constrained environments.

UX_VIS_READ_014.title: Design Overrides Default Reading Patterns
UX_VIS_READ_014.rule: Default reading patterns like the F-pattern, Z-pattern, and Gutenberg diagram primarily apply to text-heavy, design-light pages. Introducing visual hierarchy, direction, movement, and rhythm overrides these natural patterns.
UX_VIS_READ_014.detect: Conduct eye-tracking or squint tests on a UI. If the most prominent visual elements do not align with the intended user journey, the design relies too heavily on assumed reading patterns.
UX_VIS_READ_014.when_to_apply: Designing landing pages, dashboards, and complex web applications where specific user actions are desired.
UX_VIS_READ_014.when_not_to_apply: Long-form articles, text-heavy documents, or search result pages where F-pattern scanning is natural and expected.

UX_TMP_TS_YORKU_001.title: Fitts' Law: Shannon Formulation and Device Throughput
UX_TMP_TS_YORKU_001.rule: Use the Shannon formulation of Fitts' Law (ID = log2(A/W + 1)) to measure the Index of Difficulty for target acquisition, where A is amplitude (distance) and W is target width. Evaluate interaction efficiency using Throughput (TP = ID/MT), recognizing that direct input devices like touchscreens generally achieve higher throughput (~7 bits/s) than indirect devices like mice (~4-5 bits/s).
UX_TMP_TS_YORKU_001.detect: Users must perform rapid, aimed movements to acquire and select UI targets (e.g., clicking buttons, tapping icons) across different input devices.
UX_TMP_TS_YORKU_001.when_to_apply: When optimizing the size and distance of interactive targets, or when comparing the ergonomic performance (throughput) of different input modalities (e.g., touch vs. mouse).
UX_TMP_TS_YORKU_001.when_not_to_apply: When tasks are cognitively bound rather than motor-bound, when users are forced to prioritize extreme accuracy over speed (temporal constraints), or when using dwell-time selection without spatial coordinates.
UX_TMP_TS_YORKU_001.quote: The variation of Fitts' index of difficulty suggested by direct analogy with Shannon's information theorem is ID = log2(A/W + 1) ... throughput values for the mouse ranged from 3.7 bits/s to 4.9 bits/s ... The value just reported for touch input reveals a performance advantage for touch in the range of 40% to 85% compared to a mouse.

UX_TMP_ROXIMITY_001.title: Proximity Grouping via Whitespace
UX_TMP_ROXIMITY_001.rule: Ensure the whitespace between distinct UI groups is noticeably larger than the whitespace within a group to clearly communicate relationships and visual hierarchy.
UX_TMP_ROXIMITY_001.detect: Measure spacing tokens or CSS margins/padding. The gap between related elements (e.g., a label and its input, or a heading and its paragraph) must be strictly smaller than the gap separating that group from the next adjacent group.
UX_TMP_ROXIMITY_001.when_to_apply: When designing forms, navigation menus, text layouts, and responsive grids to help task-focused users quickly scan and identify related elements.
UX_TMP_ROXIMITY_001.when_not_to_apply: When elements are already strongly grouped using explicit visual boundaries (like borders or distinct background colors - Gestalt Common Region), though proximity still reinforces these boundaries.
UX_TMP_ROXIMITY_001.quote: Using varying amounts of whitespace to either unite or separate elements is key to communicating meaningful groupings.

UX_TMP_ING_FLOW_001.title: Align CTAs with Natural Reading Patterns (F/Z-Patterns)
UX_TMP_ING_FLOW_001.rule: Leverage natural reading patterns (F-pattern, Z-pattern) for text-heavy layouts, and place interactive elements (like CTAs) at the end of the user's compositional flow to prevent visual backtracking.
UX_TMP_ING_FLOW_001.detect: Identify text-heavy pages or forms. Check if the primary CTA (e.g., 'Submit' or 'Buy Now') is placed before the information required to make the decision or complete the action, forcing the user's eye to move backwards.
UX_TMP_ING_FLOW_001.when_to_apply: Apply to text-heavy pages, search results, and sequential forms where users scan in predictable F or Z patterns.
UX_TMP_ING_FLOW_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not rely solely on these patterns when a page uses strong visual hierarchy, graphics, and rhythm to intentionally create a custom compositional flow.
UX_TMP_ING_FLOW_001.quote: On a text-heavy and graphic-light page, a visitor’s eye likely follows something like a Z-pattern or F-pattern... it makes sense to place the button to search after the form field, because the natural process is to fill in the field and then click the button.

UX_TMP_LOT_FOGG_001.title: Diagnose Onboarding CTAs using B=MAP
UX_TMP_LOT_FOGG_001.rule: Ensure every critical onboarding CTA simultaneously provides Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt. If a user fails to act, diagnose the drop-off by identifying which of these three elements is missing.
UX_TMP_LOT_FOGG_001.detect: Audit onboarding drop-off points. Check if the user knows why to act (Motivation), how to act easily (Ability), and is explicitly asked to act now (Prompt).
UX_TMP_LOT_FOGG_001.when_to_apply: When designing or optimizing user onboarding flows, permission requests, or core activation events where user action is required.
UX_TMP_LOT_FOGG_001.when_not_to_apply: When actions are automated by the system or when dealing with passive informational consumption rather than interactive tasks.
UX_TMP_LOT_FOGG_001.quote: Behavior happens when Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt come together at the same time. When a behavior does not occur, at least one of those three elements is missing.

UX_TMP_HECKLIST_002.title: Minimum Contrast Ratios for Text and UI Components
UX_TMP_HECKLIST_002.rule: Maintain a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for standard text, 3:1 for large text (18pt or 14pt bold), and 3:1 for graphical objects and interactive UI components across all states.
UX_TMP_HECKLIST_002.detect: Use a WCAG contrast checker to calculate the luminosity ratio between foreground elements (text, icons, button borders, focus rings) and their adjacent backgrounds during default, hover, focus, and active states.
UX_TMP_HECKLIST_002.when_to_apply: When defining color palettes for typography, icons, form controls, buttons, and focus indicators.
UX_TMP_HECKLIST_002.when_not_to_apply: For purely decorative elements that convey no meaning, or for logos and logotypes where brand colors are strictly mandated.
UX_TMP_HECKLIST_002.quote: Text and images of text have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Large text... has a contrast ratio of at least 3:1. A contrast ratio of at least 3:1 is present for differentiating graphical objects... and author-customized interface components

UX_TMP__WAYBACK_001.title: Measure Perceived Workload using NASA-TLX Subscales
UX_TMP__WAYBACK_001.rule: Assess subjective user workload across six dimensions: Mental Demand, Physical Demand, Temporal Demand, Own Performance, Effort, and Frustration Level.
UX_TMP__WAYBACK_001.detect: Evaluating task difficulty, cognitive load, or user stress during usability testing or system evaluation.
UX_TMP__WAYBACK_001.when_to_apply: Apply when evaluating complex tasks, socio-technical systems, or when understanding the specific type of user strain (e.g., mental vs. physical vs. temporal) is necessary for UX improvements.
UX_TMP__WAYBACK_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use as a replacement for objective performance metrics (speed, accuracy). Avoid for trivial tasks where a simple Single Ease Question (SEQ) is sufficient.
UX_TMP__WAYBACK_001.quote: The formulation of Fitts's index of difficulty most frequently used... is called the Shannon formulation: ID = log2(D/W + 1)... Placing layout elements on the four edges of the screen allows for infinitely large targets in one dimension... Since the pointer will always stop at the edge, the user can move the mouse with the greatest possible speed and still hit the target.

UX_TMP_ELDGUIDE_001.title: Fitts' Law: Target Size and Distance
UX_TMP_ELDGUIDE_001.rule: Optimize target acquisition time by minimizing the distance (D) and maximizing the width (W) of interactive elements. Leverage screen edges to create 'infinite' target sizes (e.g., top-of-screen menus), and use larger targets or anchor points for interfaces in unstable environments.
UX_TMP_ELDGUIDE_001.detect: Measure the distance to and width of interactive targets to calculate the Index of Difficulty (ID). Identify if frequently used targets have a high ID, or if screen edges are underutilized for global menus.
UX_TMP_ELDGUIDE_001.when_to_apply: Apply to primary calls-to-action, frequently used navigation, and interfaces used in unstable environments (e.g., mobile devices in vehicles) where motor precision is compromised.
UX_TMP_ELDGUIDE_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to destructive or irreversible actions where adding motor friction (making the target smaller or further away) is desirable to prevent accidental activation.
UX_TMP_ELDGUIDE_001.quote: A particularly interesting example of pointing is for menus at the top of a screen... if you 'overshoot' when pointing to the top of the screen, the cursor stays at the top. This means that the size of the target is actually very big and users can be fairly careless about pointing exactly at the menu word.

UX_TMP_RING_PDF_001.title: Fitts's Law and Steering Law Optimization
UX_TMP_RING_PDF_001.rule: Minimize distance (D) and maximize target width (W) for pointing tasks (Fitts's Law: T = a + b * log2(1 + D/W)), and maximize path width for trajectory tasks like nested menus (Steering Law: T = a + b * D/W).
UX_TMP_RING_PDF_001.detect: Measure target sizes, distances between sequential interaction points, and the width of required movement corridors (e.g., nested hover menus). Flag targets < 44x44pt or narrow steering paths.
UX_TMP_RING_PDF_001.when_to_apply: When designing pointer-driven interfaces, touch targets, nested menus, scrollbars, and drag-and-drop interactions.
UX_TMP_RING_PDF_001.when_not_to_apply: When designing keyboard-only navigation, voice interfaces, or command-line tools where spatial motor movement is irrelevant.

UX_TMP_DELS_PDF_001.title: Fitts's Law for Target Acquisition
UX_TMP_DELS_PDF_001.rule: Design interactive targets to be large enough and positioned close to the user's typical cursor or resting point to minimize the time and motor effort required to acquire them.
UX_TMP_DELS_PDF_001.detect: Measure the size of clickable areas (e.g., buttons < 44x44px) and the distance between sequential interaction points.
UX_TMP_DELS_PDF_001.when_to_apply: When designing layouts with primary calls to action, navigation menus, or any interface requiring rapid, accurate pointing (mouse or touch).
UX_TMP_DELS_PDF_001.when_not_to_apply: When designing destructive actions (e.g., 'Delete Account') where adding friction (smaller target, further away) prevents accidental clicks.
UX_TMP_DELS_PDF_001.quote: Basic HCI models overview including pointing

UX_TMP_HICK_PMC_001.title: Hick-Hyman Law of Choice Entropy
UX_TMP_HICK_PMC_001.rule: Reaction time increases linearly with the information entropy (log2 of the number of response alternatives) of a choice. Minimize the number of options to reduce cognitive load and decision latency.
UX_TMP_HICK_PMC_001.detect: Count the number of mutually exclusive options presented to a user. High entropy (>4-8 options) without categorization indicates potential cognitive overload and increased decision latency.
UX_TMP_HICK_PMC_001.when_to_apply: When designing navigation menus, pricing tiers, settings panels, or any interface requiring rapid user decision-making.
UX_TMP_HICK_PMC_001.when_not_to_apply: When users are engaged in exploratory browsing, or when options are already highly categorized and familiar (e.g., alphabetical lists where users know exactly what they are looking for).
UX_TMP_HICK_PMC_001.quote: The Hick–Hyman law describes a linear increase in reaction time (RT) as a function of the information entropy of response selection, which is computed as the binary logarithm of the number of response alternatives.

UX_TMP_ISIONLAB_001.title: Hick's Law: Minimize Choices to Reduce Decision Time
UX_TMP_ISIONLAB_001.rule: Reduce the number of options presented to users at any given time to minimize cognitive load and prevent decision fatigue.
UX_TMP_ISIONLAB_001.detect: Evaluate interfaces for the number of simultaneous choices. Flag areas where users are presented with long, uncategorized lists of options.
UX_TMP_ISIONLAB_001.when_to_apply: Apply to consumer-facing interfaces, navigation menus, and onboarding flows where users need to make quick, frictionless decisions.
UX_TMP_ISIONLAB_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when designing complex tools or dashboards for domain experts who require high information density and immediate access to all options.
UX_TMP_ISIONLAB_001.quote: In short, the more options people have, the longer it takes to choose.

UX_TMP_LLECTIVE_001.title: Apply Hick-Hyman Law to Minimize Primary UI Choices
UX_TMP_LLECTIVE_001.rule: Limit the number of visible choices on primary screens to only the most crucial controls, moving advanced options to secondary menus to reduce cognitive load and decision time.
UX_TMP_LLECTIVE_001.detect: Count the number of interactive elements on a primary screen. Identify if advanced or rarely used options are cluttering the main view instead of being nested in secondary menus.
UX_TMP_LLECTIVE_001.when_to_apply: When designing interfaces for time-sensitive tasks, emergency settings, or complex systems where users need to make quick, accurate decisions without cognitive overload.
UX_TMP_LLECTIVE_001.when_not_to_apply: When users need to compare all available options simultaneously, or when hiding options significantly impairs the discoverability of frequently used features.
UX_TMP_LLECTIVE_001.quote: On the main screen of a medical device, only the most crucial controls (start, stop, pause) are visible. Advanced options are accessible through a secondary menu, which reduces the initial cognitive load.

UX_TMP_SIVE_NNG_001.title: Progressive Disclosure
UX_TMP_SIVE_NNG_001.rule: Initially show users only a few of the most important options, and defer advanced or rarely used features to a secondary screen accessible upon request.
UX_TMP_SIVE_NNG_001.detect: Check if complex forms, menus, or dialogs present all possible options at once, or if advanced/rarely used settings are hidden behind an 'Advanced' or 'More options' toggle.
UX_TMP_SIVE_NNG_001.when_to_apply: Apply when an interface has a large number of features or options, but most users only need a small core subset to complete their primary tasks.
UX_TMP_SIVE_NNG_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to frequently used core features, or when users need to frequently alternate between interdependent options that would be split across multiple screens.
UX_TMP_SIVE_NNG_001.quote: Initially, show users only a few of the most important options. Offer a larger set of specialized options upon request.

UX_TMP_ETIC_NNG_001.title: The Aesthetic-Usability Effect
UX_TMP_ETIC_NNG_001.rule: Users perceive attractive products as more usable and are more tolerant of minor usability issues when they have a positive emotional response to the visual design.
UX_TMP_ETIC_NNG_001.detect: During usability testing, observe if a user struggles to complete tasks but provides highly positive feedback focused solely on the visual design (e.g., colors, photos).
UX_TMP_ETIC_NNG_001.when_to_apply: Apply high-quality visual design to create a positive first impression, build trust, and increase user patience for minor friction points.
UX_TMP_ETIC_NNG_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not rely on aesthetics to mask severe usability issues or sacrifice core functionality for visual appeal, as users will lose patience with major blockers.
UX_TMP_ETIC_NNG_001.quote: When users have a positive emotional response to visual design, it makes them more tolerant of minor usability issues.

UX_TMP_OGROCKET_001.title: Troubleshoot Behavior Using Prompt-Ability-Motivation Sequence
UX_TMP_OGROCKET_001.rule: When diagnosing why users fail to perform a desired behavior, troubleshoot in a strict sequence: first verify the presence of a clear Prompt, next assess the user's Ability (reduce friction), and only address Motivation as the final step.
UX_TMP_OGROCKET_001.detect: Users are dropping off at a specific step in a funnel, failing to complete onboarding, or ignoring a core feature despite apparent interest.
UX_TMP_OGROCKET_001.when_to_apply: Apply during onboarding optimization, conversion rate optimization, or when debugging low feature adoption to systematically identify the behavioral bottleneck.
UX_TMP_OGROCKET_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply if the product fundamentally lacks a value proposition, as no prompt or ease-of-use will fix a complete absence of baseline motivation.
UX_TMP_OGROCKET_001.quote: start by examining the prompts... If that does not resolve the problem, move on to step 2 and analyze if the individual has the ability... focusing on motivation should always be the last step in the troubleshooting process.

UX_TMP_LIDATION_001.title: Integrate Custom Form Validation via setCustomValidity()
UX_TMP_LIDATION_001.rule: Use the Constraint Validation API's setCustomValidity() method to enforce complex form constraints (e.g., cross-field checks, file size limits) while maintaining native browser validation UI. Pass an empty string to mark the field as valid, or a descriptive error message to mark it as invalid and display the message to the user.
UX_TMP_LIDATION_001.detect: Look for custom form validation logic that manually manipulates DOM error messages and prevents submission via event.preventDefault(), instead of leveraging HTMLInputElement.setCustomValidity().
UX_TMP_LIDATION_001.when_to_apply: When standard HTML attributes (pattern, min, max) are insufficient for the validation logic (e.g., checking file sizes, comparing two password fields) but you still want to use native :valid/:invalid CSS and browser error popups.
UX_TMP_LIDATION_001.when_not_to_apply: When implementing a completely custom form validation UI that intentionally bypasses native browser tooltips (often using the novalidate attribute on the form).
UX_TMP_LIDATION_001.quote: With inline validation, users have to repeatedly switch between two quite different mental modes: form-filling and error-correcting... It’s best to keep the validation message until the user has finished with an input field and moved on to the next.

UX_TMP_EHARBOUR_001.title: Use Multi-Step Layouts for Long Forms
UX_TMP_EHARBOUR_001.rule: Split long forms into multiple steps (2-3 steps) and place sensitive fields (like email or phone) on the final step to reduce initial intimidation and leverage the sunk cost fallacy.
UX_TMP_EHARBOUR_001.detect: Single-page forms with many fields (>6) or forms asking for sensitive contact information upfront alongside other data.
UX_TMP_EHARBOUR_001.when_to_apply: When designing lead generation, onboarding, or complex data-entry forms that require significant user effort.
UX_TMP_EHARBOUR_001.when_not_to_apply: When the form is already very short (1-3 fields), such as a simple login or newsletter signup.
UX_TMP_EHARBOUR_001.quote: Splitting your forms into two or three steps will almost always increase form completion... By asking for sensitive information (email, phone) on the final step of a multi-step form, users are more likely to fill out these fields

UX_TMP_MP_AUDIT_001.title: Trigger Inline Validation on Blur or Input
UX_TMP_MP_AUDIT_001.rule: Display form validation error messages inline immediately when a user leaves a required field (on blur) or during entry (on input), rather than waiting for form submission.
UX_TMP_MP_AUDIT_001.detect: Audit required form fields (input[required], textarea[required]) to ensure they have 'blur' or 'input' event listeners attached for validation, and that error messages render in the DOM prior to form submission.
UX_TMP_MP_AUDIT_001.when_to_apply: Apply to multi-field forms (sign-up, checkout, contact) where users benefit from immediate feedback to correct errors in context.
UX_TMP_MP_AUDIT_001.when_not_to_apply: Avoid aggressive 'input' validation that flags errors before the user has finished typing a valid entry (e.g., flagging an incomplete email address as invalid while they are still typing).
UX_TMP_MP_AUDIT_001.quote: Error messages should show the message when the user leaves the field and not just at submission. Research demonstrates that even just the timing of the feedback alone significantly disrupts user performance.

UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_001.title: Avoid Reset and Clear Buttons
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_001.rule: Do not include Reset or Clear buttons in web forms to prevent accidental deletion of user input.
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_001.detect: Identify button elements with type='reset' or text labels containing 'Clear' or 'Reset'.
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_001.when_to_apply: Apply to standard web forms, data entry screens, and checkout flows.
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_001.when_not_to_apply: Forms collecting extremely sensitive input where users might explicitly need to abandon and wipe their data, though a visually de-emphasized Cancel button is preferred.
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_001.quote: The risk of accidental deletion outweighs the unlikely need to 'start over' on a web form.

UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_002.title: Single-Column Form Layout
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_002.rule: Present form fields in a single column layout to maintain the user's vertical momentum.
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_002.detect: Check if form fields are placed in multiple columns for unrelated data points.
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_002.when_to_apply: When designing standard web forms to minimize visual reorientation.
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_002.when_not_to_apply: When displaying short, logically related fields that belong together, such as City, State, and Zip Code.
UX_TMP_EB_FORMS_002.quote: Multiple columns interrupt the vertical momentum of moving down the form. Rather than requiring users to visually reorient themselves, keep them in the flow by sticking to a single column with a separate row for each field.

UX_TMP_G_ERRORS_001.title: Inline Plain-Language Error Messages
UX_TMP_G_ERRORS_001.rule: Display error messages adjacent to the affected interface element using plain, human-readable language that avoids technical jargon and user blame.
UX_TMP_G_ERRORS_001.detect: Trigger an error state on a form field. Verify that the error indicator and message appear in close proximity to the field, and that the copy uses non-technical, constructive language without blaming the user (e.g., avoiding words like 'invalid' or 'illegal').
UX_TMP_G_ERRORS_001.when_to_apply: When validating user input or displaying system-generated interruptions related to specific interface elements.
UX_TMP_G_ERRORS_001.when_not_to_apply: When the error is a global system failure (e.g., server outage) unrelated to a specific field, where a global banner or dedicated page is more appropriate.
UX_TMP_G_ERRORS_001.quote: Display the error message close to the error's source. Reduce cognitive load by displaying an error indicator adjacent to the interface where the error occurred... Error messages should be plainspoken using legible and readable text.

UX_TMP_RESPONSE_001.title: The 3 Response Time Limits (0.1s, 1s, 10s)
UX_TMP_RESPONSE_001.rule: Provide UI feedback based on response time: <0.1s feels instantaneous (no feedback needed), 0.1s–1s keeps flow of thought (no special feedback needed), >1s requires a busy indicator, and >10s requires a percent-done progress indicator and an interrupt option.
UX_TMP_RESPONSE_001.detect: Measure interaction latency. Verify that actions taking >1s display a busy indicator (e.g., cursor change) and actions taking >10s display a determinate progress bar and a cancel button.
UX_TMP_RESPONSE_001.when_to_apply: When designing interactive applications where users trigger operations requiring processing, data fetching, or network requests.
UX_TMP_RESPONSE_001.when_not_to_apply: When operations are purely background tasks that do not block the user's workflow, or when artificial delays are required for security (e.g., login throttling).
UX_TMP_RESPONSE_001.quote: 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously... 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted... 10 seconds is about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue.

UX_TMP_SIBILITY_001.title: Visibility of System Status
UX_TMP_SIBILITY_001.rule: Keep users informed about the current system state and the success of their interactions through appropriate, timely feedback.
UX_TMP_SIBILITY_001.detect: Identify interactive elements lacking visual feedback upon interaction, long-running processes without progress indicators, or background state changes that occur without user notification.
UX_TMP_SIBILITY_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all interactive elements, asynchronous processes, and relevant background state changes to ensure users feel in control.
UX_TMP_SIBILITY_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not expose irrelevant backstage technical details that do not directly impact the user's immediate decisions or goals.
UX_TMP_SIBILITY_001.quote: Ideally, systems should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time.

UX_TMP__CONTROL_001.title: Provide Clear Emergency Exits (Undo, Cancel, Exit)
UX_TMP__CONTROL_001.rule: Always provide clearly marked, easily discoverable 'emergency exits' (such as Undo, Cancel, or Close) for state-changing actions, multi-step flows, and overlays to maintain the user's locus of control.
UX_TMP__CONTROL_001.detect: Identify multi-step flows, overlays, or state-changing actions. Verify the presence of explicit 'Cancel', 'Close', or 'Undo' controls. Ensure overlays map the browser 'Back' button to the 'Close' action.
UX_TMP__CONTROL_001.when_to_apply: Apply to multi-step processes, data entry forms, settings changes, full-screen overlays, and any action that modifies system state.
UX_TMP__CONTROL_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to trivial, non-destructive navigation where the standard browser 'Back' button provides sufficient control without data loss.
UX_TMP__CONTROL_001.quote: Users often choose system functions by mistake and will need a clearly marked 'emergency exit' to leave the unwanted state without having to go through an extended dialogue. Support undo and redo.

UX_TMP__PATTERN_001.title: Prevent F-Pattern Scanning with Front-Loaded Formatting
UX_TMP__PATTERN_001.rule: Break up unformatted text using front-loaded headings, bulleted lists, bolded keywords, and descriptive links to prevent users from defaulting to the F-shaped scanning pattern and missing critical content.
UX_TMP__PATTERN_001.detect: Identify 'walls of text' lacking subheadings, bullet points, or bolded keywords, particularly where critical information is buried in the middle or right side of the text block.
UX_TMP__PATTERN_001.when_to_apply: Apply to content-heavy pages, articles, or documentation where users are likely scanning for specific answers rather than reading comprehensively.
UX_TMP__PATTERN_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to immersive storytelling or narrative content where users are highly committed to reading every word and heavy formatting would disrupt the flow.
UX_TMP__PATTERN_001.quote: Good web formatting reduces the impact of F-scanning. If your pages have big chunks of unformatted text, people will scan it in an F-shape.

UX_TMP_MILARITY_001.title: Gestalt Similarity for Control Grouping
UX_TMP_MILARITY_001.rule: Group related UI controls and signify common functionality by applying shared visual characteristics—such as color, shape, or size—while intentionally varying these traits for unrelated or differing actions.
UX_TMP_MILARITY_001.detect: Identify sets of controls or interactive elements. Verify that elements with similar functions share a distinct visual trait (e.g., color or shape) and that decorative or unrelated elements do not mimic these interactive traits.
UX_TMP_MILARITY_001.when_to_apply: When designing navigation, forms, or toolbars where users need to quickly scan and identify elements that perform similar functions or belong to the same category.
UX_TMP_MILARITY_001.when_not_to_apply: When elements are fundamentally different in function, importance, or interactivity (e.g., primary vs. secondary buttons, interactive buttons vs. decorative icons).
UX_TMP_MILARITY_001.quote: The principle of similarity simply states that when items share some visual characteristic, they are assumed to be related in some way.

UX_TMP_N_REGION_001.title: Prefer Whitespace Over Borders for Grouping
UX_TMP_N_REGION_001.rule: Use whitespace (proximity) as the primary method for grouping related elements to reduce visual clutter. Only introduce explicit boundaries (common regions like cards or borders) when whitespace is insufficient, such as when variable-length content disrupts proximity or when separating distinct functional areas.
UX_TMP_N_REGION_001.detect: Identify lists, grids, or menus where every item is enclosed in a border or card. Evaluate if removing the border and relying on the existing whitespace still clearly communicates the grouping.
UX_TMP_N_REGION_001.when_to_apply: Apply explicit boundaries (cards/borders) when elements have highly variable sizes (e.g., long wrapping titles) that break proximity, or when grouping complex, multi-element components (like recipes with images, titles, and ratings).
UX_TMP_N_REGION_001.when_not_to_apply: Avoid adding borders around simple, uniform lists or filter menus where proximity alone clearly establishes the relationship. Avoid full-width background color changes if they risk creating a 'false floor' that stops users from scrolling.
UX_TMP_N_REGION_001.quote: When possible, using whitespace alone to create clear groupings reduces the visual complexity of a design. Borders are often added in an abundance of caution... however, this approach can result in busy, cluttered designs

UX_TMP_ENREPLAY_001.title: Apply Prägnanz to Reduce Visual Density
UX_TMP_ENREPLAY_001.rule: Leverage the Gestalt principle of Prägnanz (conciseness) by maximizing negative space and removing non-essential embellishments to reduce visual density and cognitive load.
UX_TMP_ENREPLAY_001.detect: Evaluate the interface for unnecessary decorative elements, excessive text, or a lack of negative space around key focal points.
UX_TMP_ENREPLAY_001.when_to_apply: When designing complex interfaces where users need to quickly identify core messages or actions without being overwhelmed by information overload.
UX_TMP_ENREPLAY_001.when_not_to_apply: When designing data-dense analytical tools (like dashboards or spreadsheets) where high information density is explicitly required by expert users.
UX_TMP_ENREPLAY_001.quote: The principle of Prägnanz ("conciseness") is a key tenet of Gestalt psychology that states that the human brain tends to perceive visual stimuli in the simplest way possible. This implies that designs should be kept as uncluttered and streamlined as possible, without any unnecessary elements that might distract from the core message.

UX_TMP_RFOUNDRY_001.title: Apply Gestalt Principles for Visual Grouping
UX_TMP_RFOUNDRY_001.rule: Leverage the five Gestalt principles (Proximity, Similarity, Continuity, Closure, Connectedness) to organize UI elements into predictable groups, reducing visual clutter and establishing clear hierarchy without relying solely on explicit borders.
UX_TMP_RFOUNDRY_001.detect: Evaluate if related elements are grouped using whitespace (proximity), shared visual traits (similarity), or connecting lines (connectedness) rather than relying exclusively on heavy borders or explicit containers.
UX_TMP_RFOUNDRY_001.when_to_apply: Apply when organizing complex layouts, forms, or data-dense screens to help users quickly parse relationships and navigate the interface intuitively.
UX_TMP_RFOUNDRY_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not rely solely on subtle Gestalt cues if strict, unambiguous separation is required for legal, security, or severe accessibility constraints where explicit borders are necessary.
UX_TMP_RFOUNDRY_001.quote: They state that our minds have a tendency to group and organize elements and do so in predictable ways.

UX_TMP_IERARCHY_001.title: Avoid Equal Visual Weight
UX_TMP_IERARCHY_001.rule: Establish a clear visual hierarchy by varying scale, color, and contrast; avoid giving all elements or KPIs equal visual weight, as it creates visual clutter and prevents users from knowing where to focus.
UX_TMP_IERARCHY_001.detect: Identify interfaces where multiple key performance indicators (KPIs), calls to action, or content blocks share the same size, color saturation, and spacing, resulting in no clear focal point.
UX_TMP_IERARCHY_001.when_to_apply: When designing dashboards, landing pages, or complex screens that contain multiple pieces of information or actions with varying levels of importance.
UX_TMP_IERARCHY_001.when_not_to_apply: When displaying a uniform collection of items that genuinely share the exact same priority, such as a standard data table or a homogenous product grid.
UX_TMP_IERARCHY_001.quote: If everything is contrasted, then nothing stands out.

UX_TMP_XPLAINER_001.title: ISO 9241-110: Self-Descriptiveness for System Status
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_001.rule: Ensure every system status and available option is explicitly described to make the interface self-explanatory.
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_001.detect: Verify that all interactive elements have clear labels or tooltips, and that the current system state is visibly communicated to the user.
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all interactive UI components and stateful views where users need to understand current conditions or available actions.
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_001.when_not_to_apply: Avoid overly verbose descriptions in expert systems where users are highly trained and screen real estate is prioritized for data density.
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_001.quote: The system is self-explanatory - every status and every option is clearly described.

UX_TMP_XPLAINER_002.title: ISO 9241-110: Fault Tolerance via Proactive Feedback
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_002.rule: Detect and intercept errors proactively, providing immediate feedback so users can correct them without serious consequences.
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_002.detect: Check for client-side validation (e.g., mandatory field checks) and clear error messages before form submission or destructive actions.
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_002.when_to_apply: Apply during data entry, form submissions, and any user action that modifies system state or triggers external processes.
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_002.when_not_to_apply: Skip complex client-side interception if the action is trivial and instantly reversible without side effects.
UX_TMP_XPLAINER_002.quote: Errors are detected, intercepted or can be corrected without serious consequences.

UX_TMP_OGDESIGN_001.title: Positive System Status Assurance
UX_TMP_OGDESIGN_001.rule: Provide explicit, positive feedback to assure users that the system is functioning correctly and securely, rather than only surfacing feedback during errors or active processes.
UX_TMP_OGDESIGN_001.detect: Check the default or idle states of monitoring, security, or background-processing interfaces. Verify that a clear 'all clear', 'connected', or 'protected' status is visible when no user action is required.
UX_TMP_OGDESIGN_001.when_to_apply: When designing systems that run in the background, monitor security, or handle critical ongoing states (e.g., anti-virus software, cloud backups, network connectivity, or sync statuses).
UX_TMP_OGDESIGN_001.when_not_to_apply: When designing direct-manipulation tools (e.g., a text editor or drawing application) where constant 'everything is OK' messages would create unnecessary visual noise and distract from the primary task.
UX_TMP_OGDESIGN_001.quote: Assure the user that everything looks OK: An anti-virus program displays a clear assurance 'You are protected' together with a large, green checkmark and the link 'More information'.

UX_TMP_IONS_HCI_001.title: Keystroke-Level Model (KLM) Efficiency
UX_TMP_IONS_HCI_001.rule: Optimize high-frequency data input tasks by minimizing the total time of physical and mental operators, specifically keystrokes, button clicks, pointer movements, and keyboard-to-mouse shifts.
UX_TMP_IONS_HCI_001.detect: Map the user journey for a specific task and count the discrete physical operators (clicks, keystrokes, hand movements between devices) and mental pauses required to complete it.
UX_TMP_IONS_HCI_001.when_to_apply: When designing interfaces for repetitive data entry, expert systems, or high-frequency tasks where motor efficiency and execution speed are critical.
UX_TMP_IONS_HCI_001.when_not_to_apply: When designing for novice users, exploratory tasks, or complex problem-solving where discoverability and learnability outweigh raw execution speed.
UX_TMP_IONS_HCI_001.quote: It predicts task times based on a simple set of physical and mental operators including keystrokes, button clicks, pointer movement, keyboard to mouse movement, and thinking time.

UX_TMP_NASA_TLX_001.title: Measure Subjective Workload using NASA-TLX Subscales
UX_TMP_NASA_TLX_001.rule: Assess subjective user workload by measuring six specific subscales (Mental Demand, Physical Demand, Temporal Demand, Performance, Effort, Frustration) and calculating a weighted average, rather than using a single generic difficulty rating.
UX_TMP_NASA_TLX_001.detect: Review user research protocols and post-task questionnaires. Check if workload assessment relies on a single 'ease of use' question instead of the six multi-dimensional NASA-TLX dimensions.
UX_TMP_NASA_TLX_001.when_to_apply: When evaluating complex human-machine interfaces, command/control workstations, simulations, or tasks where cognitive, physical, and temporal demands vary significantly and require precise measurement.
UX_TMP_NASA_TLX_001.when_not_to_apply: When evaluating simple, low-stakes consumer web interactions where a standard System Usability Scale (SUS) or Single Ease Question (SEQ) is sufficient and lower participant friction is required.
UX_TMP_NASA_TLX_001.quote: By incorporating a multi-dimensional rating procedure, NASA TLX derives an overall workload score based on a weighted average of ratings on six subscales: Mental Demand, Physical Demand, Temporal Demand, Performance, Effort, Frustration

UX_TMP_AHRQ_TLX_001.title: Measure Subjective Mental Workload using NASA-TLX
UX_TMP_AHRQ_TLX_001.rule: Use the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) to evaluate the subjective mental workload of users performing specific tasks by measuring six dimensions: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, effort, performance, and frustration.
UX_TMP_AHRQ_TLX_001.detect: A UX evaluation or usability test requires quantifying the cognitive or physical burden of a specific workflow or task on the user.
UX_TMP_AHRQ_TLX_001.when_to_apply: When you need a standardized, generic, and validated metric to compare the mental workload of different UI designs, workflows, or tasks, especially in complex domains like healthcare.
UX_TMP_AHRQ_TLX_001.when_not_to_apply: When the task is extremely brief and administering a 6-dimension survey with 15 pairwise comparisons would be disproportionately laborious, or when interrupting the task to measure workload would invalidate time-sensitive performance metrics.
UX_TMP_AHRQ_TLX_001.quote: The NASA task load index (NASA TLX) is a tool for measuring and conducting a subjective mental workload (MWL) assessment. It allows you to determine the MWL of a participant while they are performing a task.

UX_TMP_ERCEIVED_001.title: Select the Right Usability Questionnaire (SUS, SEQ, NASA-TLX)
UX_TMP_ERCEIVED_001.rule: Use the System Usability Scale (SUS) post-test to measure overall perceived usability, the Single Ease Question (SEQ) post-task to measure specific task difficulty, and the NASA-TLX post-task to measure workload in complex, mission-critical systems.
UX_TMP_ERCEIVED_001.detect: Review usability test protocols to ensure SUS is administered at the end of the session, while SEQ or NASA-TLX are administered immediately after individual tasks.
UX_TMP_ERCEIVED_001.when_to_apply: When conducting summative quantitative studies (n >= 20-30) to benchmark usability, compare design iterations, or identify problematic workflows using standardized, validated instruments.
UX_TMP_ERCEIVED_001.when_not_to_apply: When conducting small-sample qualitative studies (e.g., 5 users) where numeric scores lack statistical significance, unless explicitly paired with qualitative follow-up questions (e.g., 'Why did you give this score?').
UX_TMP_ERCEIVED_001.quote: In most cases, use the SUS after the test and the SEQ after each task, as satisfaction metrics to complement other performance metrics... If you have the special case of complex, mission-critical workflows, replace the SEQ with NASA-TLX.

UX_TMP_INCIPLES_001.title: Cohesive Experience via Consistent Components
UX_TMP_INCIPLES_001.rule: Implement consistent language, patterns, and components across the interface so users can accomplish tasks without having to relearn how the system works.
UX_TMP_INCIPLES_001.detect: Audit the UI for the use of standardized design tokens, shared component libraries, and consistent terminology across different views or modules.
UX_TMP_INCIPLES_001.when_to_apply: When building complex platforms, enterprise software, or multi-view applications where users perform repeated workflows and rely on predictability.
UX_TMP_INCIPLES_001.when_not_to_apply: When designing distinct, standalone marketing campaigns or highly specialized, context-specific tools that require unique, non-standard interactions.
UX_TMP_INCIPLES_001.quote: Eliminate ambiguity and enable people to see, understand, and act with confidence. Streamline and optimise workflows by intelligently anticipating needs to help people work better, smarter, and faster.

UX_TMP_S_COLORS_001.title: Semantic Color Roles for Status and Purpose
UX_TMP_S_COLORS_001.rule: Assign specific semantic meanings to colors (e.g., red for critical, green for success) and use them exclusively to communicate status, urgency, or direct attention, never for mere decoration in the UI.
UX_TMP_S_COLORS_001.detect: Check CSS/styling for semantic token usage (e.g., var(--color-critical), var(--color-success)) versus hardcoded colors. Ensure color is not the sole indicator of meaning.
UX_TMP_S_COLORS_001.when_to_apply: When building UI components that communicate status, urgency, or direct user attention to specific actions or information.
UX_TMP_S_COLORS_001.when_not_to_apply: When creating standalone illustrations or marketing graphics where decorative color does not distract from core user tasks.
UX_TMP_S_COLORS_001.quote: Each usage of color within the Shopify admin is purposefully tied to a specific meaning. For instance, red signifies critical errors, green represents success messages

UX_TMP_S_DESIGN_001.title: Semantic Color Token Usage for Status and Attention
UX_TMP_S_DESIGN_001.rule: Apply color tokens purposefully to highlight important areas, communicate status and urgency, and direct user attention.
UX_TMP_S_DESIGN_001.detect: Review CSS/styling code to ensure colors are applied using semantic tokens (e.g., 'status-critical', 'interactive-primary') to convey meaning, rather than hardcoded hex values or purely decorative token usage.
UX_TMP_S_DESIGN_001.when_to_apply: When building data-rich views, action-driven interfaces, and defining the foundational design tokens for a UI library.
UX_TMP_S_DESIGN_001.when_not_to_apply: When designing standalone marketing pages or expressive illustrations where brand aesthetics take precedence over functional UI patterns.
UX_TMP_S_DESIGN_001.quote: Color highlights important areas, communicates status, urgency, and directs attention.

UX_TMP_AN_ABOUT_001.title: Use Tokens as Opinionated Building Blocks
UX_TMP_AN_ABOUT_001.rule: Implement design tokens and foundational visual styles (color, spacing, typography) as opinionated building blocks to ensure cohesive user experiences and reject infinite flexibility.
UX_TMP_AN_ABOUT_001.detect: Analyze CSS or styling code for hardcoded hex codes, absolute pixel values for spacing, or custom font definitions instead of standardized design token references.
UX_TMP_AN_ABOUT_001.when_to_apply: When developing UI components and applications that need to scale efficiently and maintain brand consistency across a larger ecosystem.
UX_TMP_AN_ABOUT_001.when_not_to_apply: When building isolated, one-off marketing pages or experimental prototypes that explicitly require diverging from the core design system.
UX_TMP_AN_ABOUT_001.quote: Create engaging user experiences with foundations. These include our tokens, guidelines, and visual styles: color, spacing, typography, and more.

UX_TMP_SSIAN_AI_001.title: AI-Legible Design System Context Layers
UX_TMP_SSIAN_AI_001.rule: Augment traditional design system infrastructure (foundations, tokens, components) with a machine-readable 'context layer' (structured content files, MCP servers, markdown schemas) to enable AI agents to accurately compose interfaces and reduce token usage.
UX_TMP_SSIAN_AI_001.detect: Look for design systems that only provide human-readable documentation without machine-readable context files (like DESIGN.md, MCP servers, or structured schemas) for LLM consumption.
UX_TMP_SSIAN_AI_001.when_to_apply: When integrating AI coding assistants, prototyping tools, or agentic workflows into a product development lifecycle that relies on a standardized design system.
UX_TMP_SSIAN_AI_001.when_not_to_apply: For small, one-off projects without a formalized design system, or when AI generation is explicitly prohibited by security or compliance policies.
UX_TMP_SSIAN_AI_001.quote: The expanded design system infra stack... includes structured content files that guide AI in better quality decision-making using fewer AI tokens, our Atlassian Design System MCP server, unified templates for code generation, building ADS skills and other markdown files for portability.

UX_TMP_X_THEMES_001.title: 12-Step Semantic Color Token Scale
UX_TMP_X_THEMES_001.rule: Structure tokenized color scales into 12 steps with specific semantic purposes: steps 1-2 for backgrounds, 3-5 for interactive component states, 6-8 for borders and separators, 9-10 for solid backgrounds/brand colors, and 11-12 for accessible text.
UX_TMP_X_THEMES_001.detect: Check color token definitions and usage. Verify if scales are divided into 12 steps and if components map their backgrounds, borders, and text to the corresponding semantic steps (e.g., text uses step 11 or 12).
UX_TMP_X_THEMES_001.when_to_apply: When designing a comprehensive, accessible design token system for a component library or complex application requiring consistent interactive states and contrast.
UX_TMP_X_THEMES_001.when_not_to_apply: When building a simple, single-theme site with minimal interactive states, or when constrained by a legacy 100-900 lightness-based color system.
UX_TMP_X_THEMES_001.quote: Each accent is a 12-step scale... /* Backgrounds */ var(--accent-1); var(--accent-2); /* Interactive components */ var(--accent-3); ... /* Borders and separators */ var(--accent-6); ... /* Solid colors */ var(--accent-9); ... /* Accessible text */ var(--accent-11);

UX_TMP_T_NNG_IA_001.title: Define Information Architecture Before Navigation UI
UX_TMP_T_NNG_IA_001.rule: Separate Information Architecture (the underlying content structure and relationships) from Navigation (the UI components used to access it). Always define the IA before selecting navigation UI patterns to ensure the UI can accommodate the full scope and depth of the content.
UX_TMP_T_NNG_IA_001.detect: Look for navigation UI patterns (e.g., inverted-L, tabs) being selected or implemented before a site map or content inventory is completed, or navigation components that artificially constrain the depth of the content.
UX_TMP_T_NNG_IA_001.when_to_apply: When designing or redesigning a website, application, or complex settings interface with multiple tiers of content and functionality.
UX_TMP_T_NNG_IA_001.when_not_to_apply: When making purely cosmetic updates to an existing UI where the underlying content structure remains completely unchanged and already fits the current navigation pattern.
UX_TMP_T_NNG_IA_001.quote: Making navigation component choices based on looks alone can force you to change an ideal IA to something that doesn’t best serve the needs of users or accommodate your content.

UX_TMP_GA_MENUS_001.title: Use Mega Menus for Large Navigation Sets
UX_TMP_GA_MENUS_001.rule: Use mega menus instead of standard scrolling dropdowns for large navigation sets. Group options logically to allow users to see all choices at a glance, reducing reliance on short-term memory.
UX_TMP_GA_MENUS_001.detect: Identify standard single-column dropdowns that require scrolling to view all navigation options, or mega menus that lack clear visual grouping.
UX_TMP_GA_MENUS_001.when_to_apply: When a site has a large number of navigation options or multiple levels of information architecture that would otherwise require scrolling in a standard dropdown.
UX_TMP_GA_MENUS_001.when_not_to_apply: When the site has a shallow information architecture with few options, or when the menu would require embedding complex GUI widgets like search boxes.
UX_TMP_GA_MENUS_001.quote: Mega menus show everything at a glance, so users can see rather than try to remember. People have enough on their minds, and messing with short-term memory reduces their ability to accomplish tasks.

UX_TMP_IDELINES_001.title: Six Core Principles for Responsible AI
UX_TMP_IDELINES_001.rule: Design agentic AI systems to uphold six core responsible AI principles: Fairness, Reliability and safety, Privacy and security, Transparency, Accountability, and Inclusiveness, while maintaining human oversight.
UX_TMP_IDELINES_001.detect: AI system design documentation and UX guidelines explicitly address fairness, reliability, privacy, transparency, accountability, and inclusiveness.
UX_TMP_IDELINES_001.when_to_apply: When designing, building, and releasing any AI technology, particularly generative or agentic AI tools that operate with autonomy or impact human users.
UX_TMP_IDELINES_001.when_not_to_apply: N/A - ethical principles generally apply to all AI systems, though the rigor of evaluation scales with the system's potential impact or risk.
UX_TMP_IDELINES_001.quote: Responsible AI is a set of steps we take to make sure that AI systems are trustworthy and uphold societal principles. It involves working through issues such as fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency and accountability.

UX_TMP_LAWSOFUX_001.title: Doherty Threshold
UX_TMP_LAWSOFUX_001.rule: Keep system response times under 400ms to ensure users do not have to wait on the computer, maintaining their productivity and flow.
UX_TMP_LAWSOFUX_001.detect: Measure the time between user input (e.g., click, tap) and the corresponding UI feedback. Flag any interactions that exceed 400 milliseconds.
UX_TMP_LAWSOFUX_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all standard UI interactions, page navigations, and state changes to maintain a seamless user experience.
UX_TMP_LAWSOFUX_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when a deliberate delay is required for security (e.g., login throttling) or to build trust by showing the system is 'working hard' on a complex task.
UX_TMP_LAWSOFUX_001.quote: Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (<400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other.

UX_TMP_FUX_HICK_001.title: Hick's Law
UX_TMP_FUX_HICK_001.rule: Minimize the number and complexity of choices to reduce user decision time and cognitive load.
UX_TMP_FUX_HICK_001.detect: Count the number of distinct interactive options presented simultaneously. Flag screens with excessive choices or complex tasks that are not broken into smaller steps.
UX_TMP_FUX_HICK_001.when_to_apply: When response times are critical, during new user onboarding, or when designing complex tasks that can be progressively disclosed.
UX_TMP_FUX_HICK_001.when_not_to_apply: When simplifying removes necessary context (simplifying to the point of abstraction) or in expert interfaces where users need immediate access to many tools.
UX_TMP_FUX_HICK_001.quote: The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices.

UX_TMP_X_MILLER_001.title: Miller's Law
UX_TMP_X_MILLER_001.rule: Organize content into smaller chunks to reduce cognitive load, rather than strictly limiting interface elements to seven items.
UX_TMP_X_MILLER_001.detect: Identify flat lists, menus, or data inputs with more than 5-9 un-grouped items, or long unbroken strings of text and numbers.
UX_TMP_X_MILLER_001.when_to_apply: When presenting complex information, long forms, or data that users need to process, understand, or hold in short-term memory.
UX_TMP_X_MILLER_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use the 'magical number seven' to justify unnecessary design limitations, such as artificially restricting broad navigation menus where scanning is preferred over memorization.
UX_TMP_X_MILLER_001.quote: Organize content into smaller chunks to help users process, understand, and memorize easily.

UX_TMP_UX_JAKOB_001.title: Jakob's Law
UX_TMP_UX_JAKOB_001.rule: Leverage existing mental models by designing interfaces that work similarly to other familiar sites, allowing users to focus on tasks rather than learning new interaction models.
UX_TMP_UX_JAKOB_001.detect: Identify non-standard UI patterns for common tasks (e.g., custom form controls, unconventional navigation placement) and evaluate if they force users to learn a new mental model.
UX_TMP_UX_JAKOB_001.when_to_apply: When designing standard UI components, navigation structures, and common workflows where industry conventions are already well-established.
UX_TMP_UX_JAKOB_001.when_not_to_apply: When the product introduces a completely novel paradigm where existing mental models do not apply, or when a new pattern provides a massive, proven efficiency gain.
UX_TMP_UX_JAKOB_001.quote: Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.

UX_TMP_X_POSTEL_001.title: Postel's Law (Robustness Principle)
UX_TMP_X_POSTEL_001.rule: Accept variable input from users and translate it to meet system requirements rather than forcing strict formatting.
UX_TMP_X_POSTEL_001.detect: Identify form inputs (e.g., phone numbers, dates, credit cards) that throw validation errors for common formatting variations like spaces or dashes instead of auto-cleaning the data.
UX_TMP_X_POSTEL_001.when_to_apply: When designing forms and data entry fields where human input naturally varies in format (e.g., phone numbers, currency, dates).
UX_TMP_X_POSTEL_001.when_not_to_apply: When strict input validation is required for security reasons (e.g., passwords, cryptographic keys) or when ambiguous input could lead to destructive actions.
UX_TMP_X_POSTEL_001.quote: Accept variable input from users, translating that input to meet your requirements, defining boundaries for input, and providing clear feedback to the user.

UX_TMP__PEAKEND_001.title: Peak-End Rule for Onboarding Flows
UX_TMP__PEAKEND_001.rule: Optimize the emotional peak and the final step of onboarding flows to be highly positive and rewarding, as users judge the overall experience based on these specific moments rather than the average of all steps.
UX_TMP__PEAKEND_001.detect: Review multi-step onboarding flows. Identify the most friction-heavy step (potential negative peak) and the final success state (end). Flag if the final step lacks clear positive reinforcement, celebration, or if stressful steps lack supportive design.
UX_TMP__PEAKEND_001.when_to_apply: When designing multi-step onboarding sequences, high-stakes user actions (e.g., launching a first campaign), or complex setup flows where user anxiety might be high.
UX_TMP__PEAKEND_001.when_not_to_apply: During repetitive, high-frequency utility tasks where users prioritize pure speed and efficiency over emotional engagement or 'delight'.
UX_TMP__PEAKEND_001.quote: People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end, rather than the total sum or average of every moment of the experience.

UX_TMP__SUMMARY_001.title: Form Error Summary Pattern
UX_TMP__SUMMARY_001.rule: Display an error summary at the top of the page on validation failure, move keyboard focus to it, and include links to the specific fields with errors. Ensure the summary text exactly matches the inline error messages.
UX_TMP__SUMMARY_001.detect: Trigger a form validation error. Verify an error summary appears at the top of the <main> container, focus shifts to it, and it contains anchor links pointing to the corresponding invalid input fields.
UX_TMP__SUMMARY_001.when_to_apply: Always show an error summary when there is a form validation error upon submission, even if there is only a single error.
UX_TMP__SUMMARY_001.when_not_to_apply: When validation is purely preventative (e.g., blocking invalid characters on keypress) without triggering a form-level submission error state.
UX_TMP__SUMMARY_001.quote: When a user makes an error, you must show both an error summary and an Error message component next to each answer that contains an error... move keyboard focus to the error summary... link to each of the answers that have validation errors

UX_TMP_XT_INPUT_001.title: Associate form hints and errors using aria-describedby
UX_TMP_XT_INPUT_001.rule: Use the aria-describedby attribute on text inputs to programmatically associate them with their corresponding hint text and error messages. Keep hint text to a single short sentence without links.
UX_TMP_XT_INPUT_001.detect: Check that <input> elements have an aria-describedby attribute matching the ID of their hint and error message containers. Ensure hint containers do not contain <a> tags.
UX_TMP_XT_INPUT_001.when_to_apply: When providing supplementary hint text or validation error messages for a text input field.
UX_TMP_XT_INPUT_001.when_not_to_apply: When the explanation requires complex, multi-sentence formatting, which should be placed outside of hint text to avoid frustrating screen reader users.
UX_TMP_XT_INPUT_001.quote: One or more element IDs to add to the aria-describedby attribute, used to provide additional descriptive information for screenreader users.

UX_TMP_ERPETUAL_001.title: Proactively Disable Invalid Actions
UX_TMP_ERPETUAL_001.rule: Prevent users from executing invalid actions by disabling controls proactively, rather than allowing the action and displaying an error message afterward.
UX_TMP_ERPETUAL_001.detect: Check if form submit buttons or critical actions remain enabled when required inputs are missing or invalid, resulting in post-click error messages instead of being disabled.
UX_TMP_ERPETUAL_001.when_to_apply: Apply when the system can deterministically evaluate the validity of an action based on current input, and the reason for the disabled state is visually obvious or clearly explained.
UX_TMP_ERPETUAL_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply if the reason for the disabled state is complex or hidden, as users may feel stuck without an explicit error message to guide their recovery.
UX_TMP_ERPETUAL_001.quote: In many interfaces, it's better to prevent users from executing an invalid action altogether than to allow it and then show an error.

UX_TMP_RR_CEDAR_001.title: Defer Error Validation to On-Change or On-Submit
UX_TMP_RR_CEDAR_001.rule: Trigger form validation errors when the user moves focus away from the input (on change/blur) or upon form submission, rather than providing real-time error feedback while the user is actively typing (on input).
UX_TMP_RR_CEDAR_001.detect: Check event listeners on form inputs. If 'onInput' or 'keyup' events trigger error state rendering before the user blurs the field, it violates this rule.
UX_TMP_RR_CEDAR_001.when_to_apply: Standard form fields where users input data (text, email, numbers) and validation requires a complete entry to be accurate.
UX_TMP_RR_CEDAR_001.when_not_to_apply: When providing positive progressive cues (e.g., password strength), indicating progress, or for extremely strict input requirements where immediate formatting correction is necessary.
UX_TMP_RR_CEDAR_001.quote: While useful for form fields with very strict input requirements, research has proven real-time validation causes more user errors and takes longer to successfully complete the form.

UX_TMP_DN_FORMS_001.title: Client-Side Form Validation for Immediate Feedback
UX_TMP_DN_FORMS_001.rule: Use client-side form validation to verify data format correctness and provide immediate feedback, helping users fill out forms correctly without frustration before server submission.
UX_TMP_DN_FORMS_001.detect: Inspect <form> elements for constraint validation attributes (e.g., required, pattern, type="email") or JavaScript event listeners that validate input and display error messages prior to submission.
UX_TMP_DN_FORMS_001.when_to_apply: Whenever a form requires specific data formats, mandatory fields, or constraints to process the request successfully.
UX_TMP_DN_FORMS_001.when_not_to_apply: When the input is entirely free-form with no formatting requirements, or when validation strictly requires server-side context (e.g., checking if a username is already taken).
UX_TMP_DN_FORMS_001.quote: Sending data is not enough — we also need to make sure that the data users enter into forms is in the correct format to process it successfully... We also want to help our users to fill out our forms correctly and not get frustrated

UX_TMP_TALS_INP_001.title: Provide Initial Visual Feedback Within 200ms
UX_TMP_TALS_INP_001.rule: Ensure the UI provides visual feedback (the next painted frame) within 200 milliseconds of any user interaction (click, tap, or keypress), even if the underlying operation requires more time to complete.
UX_TMP_TALS_INP_001.detect: Measure Interaction to Next Paint (INP) using Real User Monitoring (RUM) or the web-vitals library. Check if the 75th percentile of interaction latency is <= 200ms.
UX_TMP_TALS_INP_001.when_to_apply: Whenever a user initiates an action via click, tap, or keyboard input, especially for complex or asynchronous operations that block the main thread.
UX_TMP_TALS_INP_001.when_not_to_apply: For continuous gestures like scrolling, hovering, or zooming, which have stricter latency expectations (e.g., 16ms for 60fps) and are not measured by INP.
UX_TMP_TALS_INP_001.quote: Some interactions naturally take longer than others, but for especially complex interactions, it's important to quickly present some initial visual feedback to tell the user that something is happening.

UX_TMP_NG_TOUCH_001.title: Minimum Touch Target Size (1cm x 1cm)
UX_TMP_NG_TOUCH_001.rule: Interactive elements on touchscreens must have a minimum physical rendered size of 1cm × 1cm (0.4in × 0.4in) to ensure accurate selection and prevent accidental taps.
UX_TMP_NG_TOUCH_001.detect: Measure the physical rendered dimensions of interactive elements on the target device screen. Verify that both height and width are at least 1cm.
UX_TMP_NG_TOUCH_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all interactive elements (buttons, links, icons) on touchscreen interfaces, including mobile phones, tablets, and touch displays.
UX_TMP_NG_TOUCH_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not limit to 1cm when the context of use involves movement (walking, driving) or specific audiences (children, seniors) where even larger targets are required. Does not strictly apply to mouse-driven desktop interfaces.
UX_TMP_NG_TOUCH_001.quote: Interactive elements must be at least 1cm × 1cm (0.4in × 0.4in) to support adequate selection time and prevent fat-finger errors.

UX_TMP_NG_FITTS_001.title: Minimize Distance Between Sequential Controls
UX_TMP_NG_FITTS_001.rule: Position sequential controls (like Submit buttons) and contextual menus immediately adjacent to the user's last interaction point to minimize movement time.
UX_TMP_NG_FITTS_001.detect: Identify forms where the primary action button is placed far from the last input field (e.g., in a top header), or contextual menus that open far from their trigger (e.g., bottom sheets for top-screen icons).
UX_TMP_NG_FITTS_001.when_to_apply: When designing multi-step workflows, forms, or contextual actions where the user's pointer or finger is at a predictable prior location.
UX_TMP_NG_FITTS_001.when_not_to_apply: When an action is destructive or irreversible, requiring intentional friction, or when placing targets too close risks accidental activation due to lack of padding.
UX_TMP_NG_FITTS_001.quote: If you know that a set of controls will be clicked in a certain order, place them close to each other... For example, the Submit button in a form should be placed next to the last form field.

UX_TMP_URISTICS_001.title: Visibility of System Status
UX_TMP_URISTICS_001.rule: Keep users informed about system state through appropriate and timely feedback so they can determine next steps and build trust.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_001.detect: Trigger a system action (e.g., form submission, data loading) and verify if immediate visual or textual feedback is presented to indicate the current state.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_001.when_to_apply: Whenever a user initiates an action that takes time, changes the system state, or has consequences.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_001.when_not_to_apply: For instantaneous micro-interactions where the native physical response (like a button press state) is sufficient and additional persistent feedback would clutter the UI.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_001.quote: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.

UX_TMP_URISTICS_002.title: Constructive Error Feedback
UX_TMP_URISTICS_002.rule: Express error messages in plain language, precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution using recognizable visual treatments.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_002.detect: Trigger an error state (e.g., invalid form input, network failure) and verify if the message avoids technical jargon, clearly states the issue, and offers a recovery path.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_002.when_to_apply: Whenever the system encounters an error, invalid input, or failure state that prevents the user from completing their task.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_002.when_not_to_apply: When the error is purely internal, automatically recoverable, and does not affect the user's task or experience (in which case, fail silently).
UX_TMP_URISTICS_002.quote: Error messages should be expressed in plain language (no error codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.

UX_TMP_URISTICS_003.title: Error Prevention and Confirmation
UX_TMP_URISTICS_003.rule: Prevent problems by eliminating error-prone conditions or presenting users with a confirmation option before they commit to a high-cost action.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_003.detect: Identify high-stakes actions (e.g., delete, submit payment) and check for confirmation dialogs, undo options, or input constraints.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_003.when_to_apply: When an action has severe consequences, is difficult to reverse, or when users are prone to slips or mental model mismatches.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_003.when_not_to_apply: For low-stakes, easily reversible actions where confirmation dialogs would add unnecessary friction and interrupt the user's flow.
UX_TMP_URISTICS_003.quote: Either eliminate error-prone conditions, or check for them and present users with a confirmation option before they commit to the action.

UX_TMP_SISTENCY_001.title: Maintain Consistent Button Placement Across Multipage Forms
UX_TMP_SISTENCY_001.rule: Keep primary and secondary action buttons in consistent relative positions across all pages of a multipage form or wizard to prevent accidental actions.
UX_TMP_SISTENCY_001.detect: Identify multipage forms or wizards. Check the layout of action buttons on each page. Flag if the primary/secondary button order (e.g., left vs. right) changes between steps.
UX_TMP_SISTENCY_001.when_to_apply: When designing wizards, checkout flows, or any multipage data entry process.
UX_TMP_SISTENCY_001.when_not_to_apply: When a specific step requires a fundamentally different interaction model, such as a final destructive confirmation step that intentionally disrupts flow to force attention.
UX_TMP_SISTENCY_001.quote: Ensure consistency in the placement of form fields and buttons, especially for multipage forms or wizards.

UX_TMP_OGNITION_001.title: Promote Recognition Over Recall
