UX_TMP_OGNITION_001.rule: Design interfaces to rely on recognition rather than recall by making information, options, and interface functions visible and easily accessible.
UX_TMP_OGNITION_001.detect: Identify interactions that require users to generate answers from scratch, remember hidden gestures, or memorize upfront tutorials instead of selecting from visible options.
UX_TMP_OGNITION_001.when_to_apply: Apply to menus, search interfaces (via suggestions), task resumption (via history or recently viewed), and complex formatting tasks where users need to select from available commands.
UX_TMP_OGNITION_001.when_not_to_apply: When security necessitates recall (e.g., passwords) or when designing for extreme power users where command-line speed is prioritized over learnability.
UX_TMP_OGNITION_001.quote: How do you promote recognition? By making information and interface functions visible and easily accessible.

UX_TMP_NIMALIST_001.title: Offload Cognitive Tasks to the System
UX_TMP_NIMALIST_001.rule: Minimize extraneous cognitive load by offloading tasks from the user to the system. Re-display previously entered information, set smart defaults, and use familiar layouts to reduce the need for users to remember information or make unnecessary decisions.
UX_TMP_NIMALIST_001.detect: Identify interfaces where users must recall information from previous steps, manually enter standard data, or parse dense text instead of visual cues.
UX_TMP_NIMALIST_001.when_to_apply: When designing multi-step processes, forms, or complex transactional interfaces where users have specific constraints or goals.
UX_TMP_NIMALIST_001.when_not_to_apply: When cognitive friction is intentional (e.g., confirming a destructive action) or in educational contexts where intrinsic cognitive load is necessary for learning.
UX_TMP_NIMALIST_001.quote: Look for anything in your design that requires users to read text, remember information, or make a decision. Then look for alternatives: can you show a picture, re-display previously entered information, or set a smart default?

UX_TMP_S_LABELS_001.title: Do Not Use Placeholders as Replacements for Field Labels
UX_TMP_S_LABELS_001.rule: Always provide clear, visible labels placed outside empty form fields. Never use in-field placeholder text as the sole label for a form field.
UX_TMP_S_LABELS_001.detect: Check form fields to ensure they have an associated visible label outside the input. Verify that the placeholder attribute is not the only indicator of the field's purpose.
UX_TMP_S_LABELS_001.when_to_apply: When designing any data entry form, to ensure users can remember field requirements, check their work, recover from errors, and navigate accessibly.
UX_TMP_S_LABELS_001.when_not_to_apply: Extremely simple, ubiquitous single-field forms (like a global search box with a magnifying glass icon) where context makes the input purpose universally obvious.
UX_TMP_S_LABELS_001.quote: Rather than risk having users stumble while filling out forms or waste valuable time figuring out how they work, the best solution is to have clear, visible labels that are placed outside empty form fields.

UX_TMP_PASSWORD_001.title: Provide Clear-Text Password Visibility
UX_TMP_PASSWORD_001.rule: Allow users to see the passwords they are typing by providing a show password toggle, or default to clear text for low-risk applications.
UX_TMP_PASSWORD_001.detect: Identify input[type="password"] fields and check for an associated toggle control that changes the input type to text.
UX_TMP_PASSWORD_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all login and registration forms, particularly on mobile devices where typing is difficult and error-prone.
UX_TMP_PASSWORD_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not default to clear text for high-risk applications like banking, though a user-activated toggle should still be provided.
UX_TMP_PASSWORD_001.quote: When you make it hard for users to enter passwords you create two problems... Users make more errors when they can't see what they're typing.

UX_TMP_OX_RADIO_001.title: Checkbox vs. Radio Button Selection
UX_TMP_OX_RADIO_001.rule: Use radio buttons for mutually exclusive lists where exactly one option must be selected. Use checkboxes when users can select any number of options (zero, one, or multiple).
UX_TMP_OX_RADIO_001.detect: Identify lists of options in forms. Check if mutually exclusive options use checkboxes (violation) or if multi-select options use radio buttons (violation).
UX_TMP_OX_RADIO_001.when_to_apply: When designing forms, settings, or surveys where users must select from a predefined list of options.
UX_TMP_OX_RADIO_001.when_not_to_apply: When options are not predefined, or when the control triggers an immediate action (use action buttons instead).
UX_TMP_OX_RADIO_001.quote: Radio buttons are used when there is a list of two or more options that are mutually exclusive and the user must select exactly one choice. Checkboxes are used when there are lists of options and the user may select any number of choices, including zero, one, or several.

UX_TMP_ROPDOWNS_001.title: Avoid Dropdowns for Familiar or Easily Typed Data
UX_TMP_ROPDOWNS_001.rule: Use text input fields instead of dropdowns for highly familiar data (like birthdates) or data that is faster to type (like states or countries). Long dropdowns force users to scroll and carefully steer the mouse (violating the Steering Law/Fitts' Law), which degrades form completion speed.
UX_TMP_ROPDOWNS_001.detect: Identify <select> elements in forms used for states, countries, or dates of birth, especially those with many options requiring scrolling.
UX_TMP_ROPDOWNS_001.when_to_apply: Apply to form fields where the user already knows the answer by heart (e.g., DOB) or can type a standard abbreviation quickly (e.g., 'NY' for New York).
UX_TMP_ROPDOWNS_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when the list of valid options is small (under 10 items), highly specific, or unfamiliar to the user, making discovery necessary.
UX_TMP_ROPDOWNS_001.quote: Very long dropdowns that require scrolling make it impossible for users to see all their choices in one glance. They also require careful steering of the mouse so that it does not leave the dropdown. (This is an instance of the steering law... derived from Fitts’ law...)

UX_TMP_NG_MODAL_001.title: Modal vs. Nonmodal Dialog Usage
UX_TMP_NG_MODAL_001.rule: Use modal dialogs (which block background content) only for critical warnings, irreversible actions, or to request information essential to continuing the current process. Use nonmodal dialogs for non-critical tasks or when users need to reference background information.
UX_TMP_NG_MODAL_001.detect: Identify dialogs that disable the main interface. Flag modals used for non-essential information, complex decision-making requiring outside context, or interrupting high-stakes flows like checkout.
UX_TMP_NG_MODAL_001.when_to_apply: When designing system feedback, alerts, or data entry prompts that overlay the main interface.
UX_TMP_NG_MODAL_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use modals for newsletter signups, non-essential promotions, or when the user must reference the obscured background content to make a decision.
UX_TMP_NG_MODAL_001.quote: Modal dialogs interrupt users and demand an action. They are appropriate when user’s attention needs to be directed toward important information... nonmodal (or modeless) dialogs and windows do not disable the main content

UX_TMP_SKELETON_001.title: Skeleton Screens vs. Spinners for Perceived Performance
UX_TMP_SKELETON_001.rule: Use skeleton screens for full-page loads taking 2-10 seconds to reduce perceived wait time and cognitive load. Use spinners for single-module loads, and progress bars for loads exceeding 10 seconds. Avoid both for loads under 1 second.
UX_TMP_SKELETON_001.detect: Identify loading states in the UI. Measure expected load times and scope (full page vs. single component).
UX_TMP_SKELETON_001.when_to_apply: Apply skeleton screens for full-page or major view transitions that take between 2 and 10 seconds to load.
UX_TMP_SKELETON_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use for loads under 1 second (causes annoying flashing), loads over 10 seconds (use progress bars), single-component loads (use spinners), or background processes like file uploads.
UX_TMP_SKELETON_001.quote: Spinners are typically best used on a single module, like a video or a card which is on a dashboard. Skeleton screens... are better when the full screen is loading because the wireframe gives users a sense of what the page will look like and, thus, minimizes cognitive load.

UX_TMP_G_WIZARD_001.title: Use Wizards for Infrequent or Novice Multi-Step Tasks
UX_TMP_G_WIZARD_001.rule: Use a wizard pattern to guide users through complex, multi-step tasks if the process is performed infrequently (e.g., onboarding, setup) or by novice users. Avoid wizards for frequent tasks or expert users, as the step-by-step flow increases interaction cost and limits control.
UX_TMP_G_WIZARD_001.detect: Identify multi-step data entry flows. Check if the task is performed frequently by the same user or requires cross-referencing data across steps. If frequent or requires cross-referencing, a wizard is likely an anti-pattern.
UX_TMP_G_WIZARD_001.when_to_apply: When users are unfamiliar with a domain, lack expertise, or perform a complex process rarely (like initial account setup or onboarding), and need guided, sequential steps with branching logic.
UX_TMP_G_WIZARD_001.when_not_to_apply: When users perform the task repeatedly, need to compare information across steps, require flexible non-linear workflows, or are domain experts who need high control and efficiency.
UX_TMP_G_WIZARD_001.quote: Basically, use wizards for situations where the users are likely to be unfamiliar with the process — either because they don’t have a lot of domain expertise or because they go through that process only rarely.

UX_TMP_NG_CARDS_001.title: Use Cards for Heterogeneous Browsing, Lists for Homogeneous Scanning
UX_TMP_NG_CARDS_001.rule: Use card layouts to group heterogeneous content types for browsing, but use standard vertical lists for homogeneous items to support scannability, comparison, and higher information density.
UX_TMP_NG_CARDS_001.detect: Identify repeating item layouts. Check if space-consuming cards (with borders/shadows) are used for highly homogeneous data where users need to scan or compare attributes, rather than using a dense vertical list.
UX_TMP_NG_CARDS_001.when_to_apply: Apply card layouts when displaying dashboards, social feeds, or aggregation sites containing a variety of content types (heterogeneous items) where users are casually browsing rather than searching.
UX_TMP_NG_CARDS_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use cards when users need to search for a specific item, compare multiple options (like pricing or specs), or view highly homogeneous content.
UX_TMP_NG_CARDS_001.quote: Cards work best for collections of heterogeneous items... When presenting very homogenous items... consider using a standard vertical list of items... instead of cards to support scannability and also comparisons among items.

UX_TMP_NNG_SCAN_001.title: Design Text for Scannability
UX_TMP_NNG_SCAN_001.rule: Format web text for scanning rather than word-by-word reading by using highlighted keywords, meaningful subheadings, bulleted lists, one idea per paragraph, and the inverted pyramid style.
UX_TMP_NNG_SCAN_001.detect: Identify dense paragraphs of text lacking structural breakers like subheadings, bulleted lists, or bolded keywords, and check if paragraphs contain multiple distinct ideas.
UX_TMP_NNG_SCAN_001.when_to_apply: Apply to web pages, informational sites, and digital interfaces where users are looking for specific facts or trying to quickly understand the content.
UX_TMP_NNG_SCAN_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to immersive reading experiences like fiction, or email newsletters.
UX_TMP_NNG_SCAN_001.quote: People rarely read Web pages word by word; instead, they scan the page, picking out individual words and sentences.

UX_TMP_TA_TABLE_001.title: Limit Density in Expandable Data Table Rows
UX_TMP_TA_TABLE_001.rule: Use expandable rows for supplementary information, but if the expanded content becomes cramped or overly complex, move the information to a dedicated page, side panel, or separate data table.
UX_TMP_TA_TABLE_001.detect: A data table uses expandable rows containing complex layouts, nested tables, or dense forms.
UX_TMP_TA_TABLE_001.when_to_apply: When designing data tables that require progressive disclosure of supplementary row details.
UX_TMP_TA_TABLE_001.when_not_to_apply: When the supplementary data is simple (e.g., a few text fields) and fits comfortably within the expanded row without scrolling or complex interactions.
UX_TMP_TA_TABLE_001.quote: When the content in the expanded area feels cramped, consider taking the user to a dedicated page, side panel, or data table to view the information and complete tasks.

UX_TMP_BON_FORM_001.title: Mark Only the Minority Field Requirement Status
UX_TMP_BON_FORM_001.rule: Evaluate the overall proportion of required vs. optional fields in a form. If the majority are required, mark only the optional fields with '(optional)'. If the majority are optional, mark only the required fields with '(required)'.
UX_TMP_BON_FORM_001.detect: Count the number of required and optional fields in a form. Verify that only the minority status is explicitly labeled to prevent visual clutter.
UX_TMP_BON_FORM_001.when_to_apply: When designing forms with a mix of required and optional fields, to reduce visual noise.
UX_TMP_BON_FORM_001.when_not_to_apply: When strict legal or specific accessibility compliance mandates explicit marking of all required fields regardless of proportion.
UX_TMP_BON_FORM_001.quote: If the majority of the fields are required, mark only the optional field labels with (optional). If the majority of the fields are optional, mark only the required field labels with (required).

UX_TMP_S_BANNER_001.title: Form Error Banner Focus Management
UX_TMP_S_BANNER_001.rule: When a user submits a complex form with errors, display a critical summary banner at the top of the form and programmatically move focus to it. Never move focus to banners that appear on initial page load.
UX_TMP_S_BANNER_001.detect: Identify form submission handlers. If validation fails, verify that a summary alert/banner is rendered at the top of the form, focus is programmatically shifted to this banner, and inline errors are displayed on the specific fields.
UX_TMP_S_BANNER_001.when_to_apply: When users submit long or complex forms that result in validation errors, requiring a summary of what went wrong to assist workflows for users with disabilities.
UX_TMP_S_BANNER_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not move focus to banners if they appear on page load, or if they convey information outside the user's current workflow. Avoid for very short, single-input forms where inline errors suffice.
UX_TMP_S_BANNER_001.quote: When merchants submit long or complex forms with errors, use a critical banner to summarize what went wrong. Place the banner at the top of the form and move focus to the banner when the form is submitted.

UX_TMP_K_BUTTON_001.title: Prevent Accidental Double-Clicks on Submit Buttons
UX_TMP_K_BUTTON_001.rule: Implement double-click prevention on form submit buttons to protect users with motor impairments (e.g., hand tremors) from accidentally submitting information multiple times.
UX_TMP_K_BUTTON_001.detect: Inspect form submit buttons for debounce logic, immediate disabled states upon click, or specific attributes like `data-prevent-double-click`.
UX_TMP_K_BUTTON_001.when_to_apply: Apply to form submission buttons where duplicate submissions would cause errors, duplicate records, or trigger multiple irreversible actions (e.g., sending emails, processing payments).
UX_TMP_K_BUTTON_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to standard navigation links or buttons that do not trigger state changes or data submission.
UX_TMP_K_BUTTON_001.quote: Sometimes, users double click buttons because they... have motor impairments such as hand tremors which cause them to click the button involuntarily... you can configure the button to ignore the second click.

UX_TMP_ECKBOXES_001.title: Group Checkboxes with Fieldset and Legend
UX_TMP_ECKBOXES_001.rule: Always group related checkboxes within a `<fieldset>` element and use a `<legend>` to describe the group (usually the question being asked). If the group is the only question on the page, make the `<legend>` the page heading.
UX_TMP_ECKBOXES_001.detect: Identify groups of `<input type="checkbox">` elements sharing the same `name` attribute. Verify they are wrapped in a `<fieldset>` and that the `<fieldset>` contains a valid `<legend>`.
UX_TMP_ECKBOXES_001.when_to_apply: When presenting a list of multiple related checkbox options that answer a single question or belong to a single category.
UX_TMP_ECKBOXES_001.when_not_to_apply: When a single standalone checkbox is used for a boolean toggle (e.g., 'I agree to the terms and conditions'), which does not require a fieldset grouping.
UX_TMP_ECKBOXES_001.quote: Group checkboxes together in a <fieldset> with a <legend> that describes them, as shown in the examples on this page. This is usually a question, like ‘How would you like to be contacted?’.

UX_TMP_SPONSIVE_001.title: Responsive Web Design Foundations
UX_TMP_SPONSIVE_001.rule: Use fluid grids, flexible images, and media queries to create a single, adaptive layout that responds to the user's viewport, rather than building separate device-specific experiences.
UX_TMP_SPONSIVE_001.detect: Identify fixed-width containers that overflow on small screens, or the presence of device-specific redirects (e.g., m.domain.com) instead of CSS media queries.
UX_TMP_SPONSIVE_001.when_to_apply: When building web interfaces that will be accessed across a gradient of different devices, screen sizes, and resolutions.
UX_TMP_SPONSIVE_001.when_not_to_apply: When the user goals for a specific device (like mobile) are drastically limited or different in scope, making a separate, highly tailored application more appropriate.
UX_TMP_SPONSIVE_001.quote: Rather than tailoring disconnected designs to each of an ever-increasing number of web devices, we can treat them as facets of the same experience.

UX_TMP_ESTHETIC_001.title: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
UX_TMP_ESTHETIC_001.rule: Leverage aesthetically pleasing design to increase perceived usability and user tolerance for minor friction, but use low-fidelity prototypes during early usability testing to prevent aesthetics from masking functional flaws.
UX_TMP_ESTHETIC_001.detect: Evaluate visual polish (spacing, typography, color). In usability testing, observe if users express positive sentiment or rate the system as 'easy to use' despite failing or struggling with core tasks.
UX_TMP_ESTHETIC_001.when_to_apply: When launching products where first impressions, brand trust, and user tolerance for minor friction are critical to adoption and retention.
UX_TMP_ESTHETIC_001.when_not_to_apply: During early-stage usability testing where the primary goal is to identify and fix core functional, architectural, and navigational issues.
UX_TMP_ESTHETIC_001.quote: Visually pleasing design can mask usability problems and prevent issues from being discovered during usability testing.

UX_TMP__DOHERTY_001.title: Doherty Threshold (400ms Feedback)
UX_TMP__DOHERTY_001.rule: Provide system feedback within 400 milliseconds of a user action to maintain attention and maximize productivity; use perceived performance techniques like progress bars or animations if the actual process takes longer.
UX_TMP__DOHERTY_001.detect: Measure the latency between user input events (e.g., click, submit) and the initial visual UI update. Flag interactions exceeding 400ms that lack loading indicators or optimistic updates.
UX_TMP__DOHERTY_001.when_to_apply: Apply to standard interactive elements like buttons, form submissions, navigation, and search queries where users expect continuous flow and immediate acknowledgment.
UX_TMP__DOHERTY_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when an instant response might erode user trust in a complex or high-stakes process (e.g., fraud checks, mortgage approvals), where a purposeful delay increases perceived value.
UX_TMP__DOHERTY_001.quote: Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (<400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other.

UX_TMP_X_SERIAL_001.title: Serial Position Effect
UX_TMP_X_SERIAL_001.rule: Place the most important items or key actions at the beginning and end of a list or navigation sequence, relegating the least important items to the middle.
UX_TMP_X_SERIAL_001.detect: Analyze navigation bars, menus, and lists. Verify that primary actions are positioned at the far left or far right, rather than in the middle.
UX_TMP_X_SERIAL_001.when_to_apply: Apply to navigation menus, feature lists, and action bars where specific items require higher user recall and engagement.
UX_TMP_X_SERIAL_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when the list requires a strict chronological, alphabetical, or sequential logical order that supersedes priority.
UX_TMP_X_SERIAL_001.quote: Users have a propensity to best remember the first and last items in a series.

UX_TMP_TRUCTIVE_001.title: Require Beneficial Friction for Destructive Actions
UX_TMP_TRUCTIVE_001.rule: Use specific confirmation dialogs or nonstandard actions (like typing a confirmation word) for destructive or irreversible actions, but avoid them for routine tasks to prevent habituation.
UX_TMP_TRUCTIVE_001.detect: Identify destructive actions (e.g., delete, cancel). Check if a confirmation dialog exists, uses specific action labels (not just Yes/No), lacks a default 'Yes', and for highly destructive actions, requires a nonstandard input (e.g., typing 'DELETE').
UX_TMP_TRUCTIVE_001.when_to_apply: When an action has serious consequences, destroys user work, costs significant money, or cannot be undone.
UX_TMP_TRUCTIVE_001.when_not_to_apply: For routine, easily reversible, or low-stakes actions where frequent interruptions cause alert fatigue.
UX_TMP_TRUCTIVE_001.quote: For particularly dangerous operations, require a nonstandard action from the user to confirm... have people do something they would normally not do. For example, type a word into a box...

UX_TMP__FILTERS_001.title: Faceted Navigation vs. Simple Filters
UX_TMP__FILTERS_001.rule: Use faceted navigation (multiple dimensional filters) for large, complex product catalogs to improve findability, but rely on simple filters for smaller sets to minimize interaction cost.
UX_TMP__FILTERS_001.detect: Evaluate product listing or search results pages: identify if the filtering UI offers multiple distinct dimensions (facets) or just basic, single-dimension filters.
UX_TMP__FILTERS_001.when_to_apply: Apply faceted navigation when users need to narrow down extremely large content sets across multiple distinct dimensions (e.g., e-commerce product catalogs with size, color, brand).
UX_TMP__FILTERS_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use faceted navigation if the content set is small or users only need one or two basic criteria, as it adds unnecessary cognitive load and metadata maintenance.
UX_TMP__FILTERS_001.quote: The extra power of faceted navigation also adds interaction cost by presenting users with more options to comprehend and manipulate. A simple filter can often be easier to understand and faster to use.

UX_TMP_G_STICKY_001.title: Evaluate Sticky Header Utility vs. Screen Real Estate
UX_TMP_G_STICKY_001.rule: Implement sticky headers only if navigation elements are frequently needed mid-scroll. To prevent obscuring focus, maximize the content-to-chrome ratio, ensure high contrast with an opaque background, and avoid distracting animations.
UX_TMP_G_STICKY_001.detect: Identify sticky headers on scroll. Measure the vertical height consumed (content-to-chrome ratio), check for background opacity, and assess if the persistent elements (e.g., login, search, main nav) are contextually required mid-page.
UX_TMP_G_STICKY_001.when_to_apply: Apply when users frequently jump between categories, use search, or access utility navigation (like a shopping cart) from deep within a scrolling page.
UX_TMP_G_STICKY_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when users typically consume content linearly without needing to navigate away, or when the header elements are rarely used mid-session.
UX_TMP_G_STICKY_001.quote: Sticky headers can be a positive addition to a site, but only if they truly serve a purpose for your users. If a sticky header does provide value to users, then ensure that it is as small as reasonably possible, it has high contrast against the background, does not use gratuitous animation, does not obscure content, and does not distract your users.

UX_TMP_CORDIONS_001.title: Accordions for Progressive Disclosure
UX_TMP_CORDIONS_001.rule: Use accordions to progressively disclose content only when users need a few specific pieces of information. If users need to consume most of the content, expose it all at once to avoid the cognitive load and interaction cost of repeated clicking.
UX_TMP_CORDIONS_001.detect: Identify accordions on desktop interfaces. Evaluate if the user task requires opening most panels. Verify if multiple panels can remain open simultaneously.
UX_TMP_CORDIONS_001.when_to_apply: Apply when users only need a few key pieces of content on a single page, or on mobile devices where screen space is limited and a mini-IA aids navigation.
UX_TMP_CORDIONS_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when the audience needs most or all of the content to answer their questions, or when printing the full content is a common use case.
UX_TMP_CORDIONS_001.quote: Every single decision, no matter how minor or how easy, adds cognitive load.

UX_TMP_LTIP_USE_001.title: Do Not Hide Vital Information in Tooltips
UX_TMP_LTIP_USE_001.rule: Never use tooltips to display information that is essential for task completion, such as password requirements or field instructions. Vital information must always be visible on the screen.
UX_TMP_LTIP_USE_001.detect: Identify tooltips in the UI. Check if the content inside the tooltip contains actionable instructions, constraints, or requirements necessary to complete the current task.
UX_TMP_LTIP_USE_001.when_to_apply: When designing forms, complex inputs, or any UI where specific constraints or instructions must be followed to successfully complete a task.
UX_TMP_LTIP_USE_001.when_not_to_apply: When providing supplementary, non-essential context (e.g., explaining why a piece of information is requested) or labeling ambiguous icons.
UX_TMP_LTIP_USE_001.quote: Users shouldn’t need to find a tooltip in order to complete their task. Remember that tooltips disappear, so instructions or other directly actionable information, like field requirements, shouldn’t be in a tooltip.

UX_TMP_NG_ICONS_001.title: Always Accompany Icons with Visible Text Labels
UX_TMP_NG_ICONS_001.rule: Icons must be accompanied by a visible text label at all times to clarify their meaning and reduce ambiguity. Do not rely on hover states to reveal labels.
UX_TMP_NG_ICONS_001.detect: Identify standalone icons in the UI. Check if they have accompanying text labels visible by default without requiring hover or tap interactions.
UX_TMP_NG_ICONS_001.when_to_apply: When using icons in graphical user interfaces, particularly for navigation, actions, or features that are not universally standardized.
UX_TMP_NG_ICONS_001.when_not_to_apply: When using the rare universally recognized icons (e.g., magnifying glass for search) in highly constrained spaces, though even then labels are safer.
UX_TMP_NG_ICONS_001.quote: To help overcome the ambiguity that almost all icons face, a text label must be present alongside an icon to clarify its meaning in that particular context. Icon labels should be visible at all times, without any interaction from the user.

UX_TMP_FICATION_001.title: Inline vs. Toast Notifications
UX_TMP_FICATION_001.rule: Use inline notifications for persistent, contextual feedback within a task flow. Use toast notifications for short, time-based, non-modal messages that automatically dismiss.
UX_TMP_FICATION_001.detect: Identify the notification behavior and placement: if it auto-dismisses and floats over the UI (usually top right), it should be a toast. If it persists within the page layout near related content, it should be inline.
UX_TMP_FICATION_001.when_to_apply: Use inline notifications for form errors, task statuses, or when the message must persist until resolved. Use toast notifications for quick, non-critical confirmations (e.g., 'Saved successfully') that do not require user interaction.
UX_TMP_FICATION_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use toast notifications for critical errors or messages requiring user action, as they may disappear before the user reads them. Do not use inline notifications for global, transient system updates.
UX_TMP_FICATION_001.quote: Inline notifications show up in task flows to notify users of the status of an action... Toast notifications are non-modal, time-based window elements used to display short messages; they usually appear at the top of the screen and disappear after a few seconds.

UX_TMP_ON_MODAL_001.title: Modal Complexity and Density Limits
UX_TMP_ON_MODAL_001.rule: Avoid using modals for highly repeatable tasks, complex flows, or content that exceeds the maximum height of a large modal; use a full page instead.
UX_TMP_ON_MODAL_001.detect: Identify modals containing multi-step complex flows, excessive vertical scrolling, or tasks that users must perform repeatedly in their primary workflow.
UX_TMP_ON_MODAL_001.when_to_apply: When designing enterprise workflows where users need to input dense data, make complex choices, or perform frequent repetitive actions.
UX_TMP_ON_MODAL_001.when_not_to_apply: For short, non-frequent tasks, critical immediate feedback, or simple confirmations where context retention of the underlying page is strictly required.
UX_TMP_ON_MODAL_001.quote: If a user needs to repeatably perform a task, consider making the task completable on the main page. [...] For complex flows with complex choices, consider using a full page instead of a modal.

UX_TMP_N_BUTTON_001.title: Uniform Width for Button Groups
UX_TMP_N_BUTTON_001.rule: Apply the same width to all related buttons in a group (excluding ghost buttons), typically matching the width of the button with the longest label.
UX_TMP_N_BUTTON_001.detect: Identify adjacent buttons within a button group container (e.g., primary and secondary pairs). Measure their rendered widths and flag if the widths are not equal.
UX_TMP_N_BUTTON_001.when_to_apply: When placing multiple related buttons next to each other in forms, dialogs, or standard layouts to improve visual rhythm and provide predictable hit targets.
UX_TMP_N_BUTTON_001.when_not_to_apply: When using ghost buttons, icon-only buttons, or when buttons are fluidly spanning a container as a percentage (e.g., 50% each in a narrow mobile view).
UX_TMP_N_BUTTON_001.quote: When using groups of related buttons (not including ghost buttons), they should all be the same width. The width of all the buttons is usually determined by the longest button label.

UX_TMP_DS_TOUCH_001.title: Standardize Tap Target Sizing with SLDS Tokens
UX_TMP_DS_TOUCH_001.rule: Use SLDS sizing tokens (e.g., $square-icon-medium for 32px, $square-icon-large-boundary for 48px) to define tap target boundaries and ensure consistent motor ergonomics instead of hardcoding pixel values.
UX_TMP_DS_TOUCH_001.detect: Look for hardcoded pixel values (e.g., width: 32px, height: 48px) on interactive elements (buttons, icons) instead of SLDS sizing tokens.
UX_TMP_DS_TOUCH_001.when_to_apply: When building interactive components (buttons, icon buttons, avatars) within the Salesforce Lightning ecosystem or when adopting a token-based design system for consistent hit areas.
UX_TMP_DS_TOUCH_001.when_not_to_apply: When sizing non-interactive, purely decorative elements where hit area size does not impact motor ergonomics.

UX_TMP_S_LAYOUT_001.title: Use Layout Primitives for Spacing and Alignment
UX_TMP_S_LAYOUT_001.rule: Handle all layouts and spacing using dedicated layout primitives (e.g., Box, Block stack, Inline stack, Grid) rather than embedding custom CSS margins, padding, or flex/grid properties within feature components.
UX_TMP_S_LAYOUT_001.detect: Scan for custom CSS classes, inline styles, or styled-components applying 'margin', 'padding', 'display: flex', or 'display: grid' in feature components instead of using imported layout primitive components.
UX_TMP_S_LAYOUT_001.when_to_apply: When arranging elements on a page, managing spacing between components, or building responsive layouts within a design system that provides layout primitives.
UX_TMP_S_LAYOUT_001.when_not_to_apply: When building the foundational layout primitives themselves, or when working in a legacy codebase without a standardized set of layout components.
UX_TMP_S_LAYOUT_001.quote: All layouts and spacing should be handled using layout primitives. This keeps our components simple, flexible and composable.

UX_TMP__SPACING_001.title: Use Whitespace and Scale to Establish Visual Hierarchy
UX_TMP__SPACING_001.rule: Vary the amount of whitespace and the scale of elements to rank UI components, grouping related items closer together and isolating important elements to draw focus.
UX_TMP__SPACING_001.detect: Check if all elements on a page have uniform spacing and sizing. If everything has the same visual weight and spacing, hierarchy is missing.
UX_TMP__SPACING_001.when_to_apply: When designing layouts with multiple distinct sections, actions, or data points where users need to scan and process information in a specific order.
UX_TMP__SPACING_001.when_not_to_apply: When displaying a homogeneous list or grid of equally important items (e.g., a data table), where uniform spacing is needed to group by similarity.
UX_TMP__SPACING_001.quote: Hierarchy is used to rank elements and influence the order in which users view them. [...] varying the amount of whitespace around an element can be used to group elements together or separate them to impart greater importance.

UX_TMP_AN_COLOR_001.title: Use Semantic Color Roles Instead of Accents for Meaningful UI
UX_TMP_AN_COLOR_001.rule: Apply semantic color role tokens (e.g., success, warning, danger, information) rather than generic accent tokens when a color is intended to convey specific meaning or status.
UX_TMP_AN_COLOR_001.detect: Identify design token usage (e.g., `color.background.accent.red`) on components like alerts, badges, or validation messages. Flag if an accent token is used instead of a semantic token (e.g., `color.background.danger`).
UX_TMP_AN_COLOR_001.when_to_apply: When assigning color tokens to UI elements that communicate system status, outcomes, or alerts.
UX_TMP_AN_COLOR_001.when_not_to_apply: When coloring elements that have no specific meaning tied to them, where exchanging one color for another would leave the experience unchanged (e.g., user avatars, generic tags).
UX_TMP_AN_COLOR_001.quote: Don’t use an accent when the color has semantic meaning.

UX_TMP__MESSAGE_001.title: Per-Field Error Message Pattern
UX_TMP__MESSAGE_001.rule: Display validation error messages directly above the affected input (after the label and hint text) in red, apply a red border to the input field, prepend a visually hidden 'Error:' prefix for screen readers, and preserve the user's invalid input.
UX_TMP__MESSAGE_001.detect: Trigger a form validation error. Verify the error text appears between the label/hint and the input field, the input has a red border, the original input value is retained, and a visually hidden 'Error:' span precedes the message text.
UX_TMP__MESSAGE_001.when_to_apply: When a user submits a form containing field-level validation errors.
UX_TMP__MESSAGE_001.when_not_to_apply: When the error is a system failure, lack of capacity, or eligibility issue rather than a correctable user input error.
UX_TMP__MESSAGE_001.quote: For each error: put the message in red after the question text and hint text... use a red border to visually connect the message and the question it belongs to... Do not clear any form fields when showing the Error message component.

UX_TMP_FIELDSET_001.title: Group Related Form Inputs with Fieldset
UX_TMP_FIELDSET_001.rule: Use a <fieldset> to group related form inputs, and ensure the first element inside is a <legend> that describes the group.
UX_TMP_FIELDSET_001.detect: Identify groups of related inputs (e.g., address fields, date parts). Check if they are wrapped in a <fieldset> and if the first child is a <legend>.
UX_TMP_FIELDSET_001.when_to_apply: When you need to show a relationship between multiple form inputs, such as asking for an address or presenting a group of checkboxes/radios.
UX_TMP_FIELDSET_001.when_not_to_apply: When an input is standalone and its purpose is fully described by its own <label>.
UX_TMP_FIELDSET_001.quote: Use the fieldset component when you need to show a relationship between multiple form inputs.

UX_TMP_K_RADIOS_001.title: Group Radios with Fieldset and Legend
UX_TMP_K_RADIOS_001.rule: Group related radio buttons within a <fieldset> element and use a <legend> to describe the group. If the radio group is the only question on the page, set the <legend> as the page heading (<h1>).
UX_TMP_K_RADIOS_001.detect: Identify groups of <input type='radio'> sharing the same name attribute. Verify they are enclosed in a <fieldset> containing a <legend>. If it is the sole form control on the page, verify the <legend> contains an <h1>.
UX_TMP_K_RADIOS_001.when_to_apply: When presenting a list of mutually exclusive radio button options to a user.
UX_TMP_K_RADIOS_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not set the <legend> as the page heading if there are multiple questions on the page. Do not use radios if users can select multiple options.
UX_TMP_K_RADIOS_001.quote: Group radios together in a <fieldset> with a <legend> that describes them. This is usually a question, like 'Where do you live?'.

UX_TMP_RIA_LIVE_001.title: Use ARIA Live Regions for Status Updates Without Moving Focus
UX_TMP_RIA_LIVE_001.rule: Use `aria-live="polite"` or `role="status"` to announce dynamic, non-interactive status updates to assistive technologies without forcing a page reload or moving the user's focus.
UX_TMP_RIA_LIVE_001.detect: Identify dynamic DOM updates (e.g., search results, toast notifications, status messages) that do not receive focus. Verify they are wrapped in an element with `aria-live="polite"` or `role="status"` present in the DOM before the update occurs.
UX_TMP_RIA_LIVE_001.when_to_apply: Apply when a part of the page updates dynamically with information useful to the user (e.g., search results loaded, form saved) but doesn't require immediate interaction or focus management.
UX_TMP_RIA_LIVE_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when the update requires immediate user interaction (move focus instead), or when the update is a critical error that must interrupt the user immediately (use `aria-live="assertive"` or `role="alert"`).
UX_TMP_RIA_LIVE_001.quote: Using JavaScript, it is possible to dynamically change parts of a page without requiring the entire page to reload... ARIA live regions fill this gap and provide a way to programmatically expose dynamic content changes in a way that can be announced by assistive technologies.

UX_TMP_IM_FORMS_001.title: Associate Form Instructions via aria-describedby
UX_TMP_IM_FORMS_001.rule: Use aria-describedby to programmatically associate inline instructions or helper text with specific form fields, ensuring screen readers announce them during Tab navigation.
UX_TMP_IM_FORMS_001.detect: Identify form inputs with adjacent helper text. Verify the input has an aria-describedby attribute matching the ID of the helper text element.
UX_TMP_IM_FORMS_001.when_to_apply: When a form field has specific formatting requirements, cues, or instructions located near the input field.
UX_TMP_IM_FORMS_001.when_not_to_apply: When instructions are general and placed at the very beginning of the form, or when the <label> text already fully encapsulates the instruction.
UX_TMP_IM_FORMS_001.quote: Although labels are announced when form inputs received keyboard focus, other text between the form controls is usually skipped. Be sure to include any instructions at the beginning of the form, or associate them with specific fields using aria-describedby.

UX_TMP_L_MODELS_001.title: Conform to Mental Model Inertia
UX_TMP_L_MODELS_001.rule: Design interfaces that conform to users' pre-existing mental models formed by their experiences on other websites, rather than inventing new interaction styles, unless the new approach is demonstrably superior.
UX_TMP_L_MODELS_001.detect: Identify novel interaction patterns, custom navigation behaviors (e.g., hijacking the back button), or unexpected e-commerce flows (e.g., auto-adding items) that deviate from standard web conventions.
UX_TMP_L_MODELS_001.when_to_apply: When designing core navigation, standard e-commerce flows (like shopping carts), search functionalities, and basic UI controls.
UX_TMP_L_MODELS_001.when_not_to_apply: When a new interaction paradigm is clearly superior, thoroughly tested, and accompanied by sufficient onboarding or skeuomorphism to help users build a new mental model.
UX_TMP_L_MODELS_001.quote: There's great inertia in users' mental models: stuff that people know well tends to stick, even when it's not helpful. This alone is an argument for being conservative and not coming up with new interaction styles.

UX_TMP_NABILITY_001.title: The Five Components of Usability
UX_TMP_NABILITY_001.rule: Evaluate user interfaces against the five core components of usability: learnability (first-time ease), efficiency (speed after learning), memorability (ease of returning), errors (frequency, severity, and recovery), and satisfaction (pleasantness).
UX_TMP_NABILITY_001.detect: Check if usability evaluations and metrics explicitly account for learnability, efficiency, memorability, error rates, and user satisfaction, rather than just binary task success.
UX_TMP_NABILITY_001.when_to_apply: When defining usability metrics, planning user tests, or evaluating the overall quality of a user interface.
UX_TMP_NABILITY_001.when_not_to_apply: When evaluating pure utility (whether the system has the required features) or underlying technical performance independent of the user interface.
UX_TMP_NABILITY_001.quote: Usability is defined by 5 quality components: Learnability... Efficiency... Memorability... Errors... Satisfaction...

UX_TMP_RESTORFF_001.title: Isolation Effect for Primary CTA Emphasis
UX_TMP_RESTORFF_001.rule: Make primary key actions visually distinctive from surrounding elements to ensure they are easily identified and remembered, while exercising restraint to prevent visual competition.
UX_TMP_RESTORFF_001.detect: Check if the primary CTA has a unique visual treatment (e.g., contrasting background color, size, or shape) compared to secondary buttons or surrounding elements, without relying solely on color.
UX_TMP_RESTORFF_001.when_to_apply: When there is a clear primary action or critical information that users need to find and remember among a group of similar items.
UX_TMP_RESTORFF_001.when_not_to_apply: When all actions have equal priority, or when overusing emphasis would cause visual competition and make elements look like advertisements.
UX_TMP_RESTORFF_001.quote: The Von Restorff effect, also known as The Isolation Effect, predicts that when multiple similar objects are present, the one that differs from the rest is most likely to be remembered.

UX_TMP_E_TOGGLE_001.title: Inclusive Toggle Button Pattern
UX_TMP_E_TOGGLE_001.rule: Implement toggle buttons using `<button>` elements with `aria-pressed` or `role="switch"` and `aria-checked`. Never change the text label (e.g., 'Play' to 'Pause') and the ARIA state simultaneously.
UX_TMP_E_TOGGLE_001.detect: Check if a toggle control uses a `<button>` element with `aria-pressed` or `role="switch"` + `aria-checked`. Verify via DOM mutation observers or code inspection that the button's text content and its ARIA state attribute do not toggle at the same time.
UX_TMP_E_TOGGLE_001.when_to_apply: When creating custom on/off switches or toggle buttons that change interface state instantaneously without submitting form data.
UX_TMP_E_TOGGLE_001.when_not_to_apply: When the control is part of a standard form data collection process, where native `<input type="checkbox">` or `<input type="radio">` are more appropriate and expected by users.
UX_TMP_E_TOGGLE_001.quote: As a rule of thumb, you should never change pressed state and label together. If the label changes, the button has already changed state in a sense, just not via explicit WAI-ARIA state management.

UX_COG_AESTHETICUSA_001.title: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
UX_COG_AESTHETICUSA_001.rule: Leverage aesthetically pleasing design to increase perceived usability, build trust, and improve user tolerance for minor friction, but use low-fidelity prototypes during early testing to prevent aesthetics from masking functional flaws.
UX_COG_AESTHETICUSA_001.detect: During usability testing, observe if users struggle to complete core tasks but still provide highly positive feedback or rate the system as 'easy to use' based primarily on visual design elements like colors and typography.
UX_COG_AESTHETICUSA_001.when_to_apply: When launching products where first impressions, brand trust, and user patience for minor friction points are critical to adoption and retention.
UX_COG_AESTHETICUSA_001.when_not_to_apply: During early-stage usability testing where the goal is to identify core functional issues, or when attempting to mask severe usability blockers, as aesthetics cannot compensate for major failures.
UX_COG_AESTHETICUSA_001.quote: When users have a positive emotional response to visual design, it makes them more tolerant of minor usability issues.

UX_AGT_AILEGIBLEDES_001.title: AI-Legible Design System Context Layers
UX_AGT_AILEGIBLEDES_001.rule: Augment traditional design system infrastructure (foundations, tokens, components) with a machine-readable 'context layer' (structured content files, MCP servers, markdown schemas) to enable AI agents to accurately compose interfaces and reduce token usage.
UX_AGT_AILEGIBLEDES_001.detect: Look for design systems that only provide human-readable documentation without machine-readable context files (like DESIGN.md, MCP servers, or structured schemas) for LLM consumption.
UX_AGT_AILEGIBLEDES_001.when_to_apply: When integrating AI coding assistants, prototyping tools, or agentic workflows into a product development lifecycle that relies on a standardized design system.
UX_AGT_AILEGIBLEDES_001.when_not_to_apply: For small, one-off projects without a formalized design system, or when AI generation is explicitly prohibited by security or compliance policies.
UX_AGT_AILEGIBLEDES_001.quote: The expanded design system infra stack... includes structured content files that guide AI in better quality decision-making using fewer AI tokens, our Atlassian Design System MCP server, unified templates for code generation, building ADS skills and other markdown files for portability.

UX_AGT_RESPONSIBLEA_001.title: Six Core Principles for Responsible AI
UX_AGT_RESPONSIBLEA_001.rule: Design agentic AI systems to uphold six core responsible AI principles: Fairness, Reliability and safety, Privacy and security, Transparency, Accountability, and Inclusiveness, while maintaining human oversight.
UX_AGT_RESPONSIBLEA_001.detect: AI system design documentation and UX guidelines explicitly address fairness, reliability, privacy, transparency, accountability, and inclusiveness.
UX_AGT_RESPONSIBLEA_001.when_to_apply: When designing, building, and releasing any AI technology, particularly generative or agentic AI tools that operate with autonomy or impact human users.
UX_AGT_RESPONSIBLEA_001.when_not_to_apply: N/A - ethical principles generally apply to all AI systems, though the rigor of evaluation scales with the system's potential impact or risk.
UX_AGT_RESPONSIBLEA_001.quote: Responsible AI is a set of steps we take to make sure that AI systems are trustworthy and uphold societal principles. It involves working through issues such as fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency and accountability.

UX_PRD_FACETEDNAVIG_001.title: Faceted Navigation vs. Simple Filters
UX_PRD_FACETEDNAVIG_001.rule: Use faceted navigation (multiple dimensional filters) for large, complex product catalogs to improve findability, but rely on simple filters for smaller sets to minimize interaction cost.
UX_PRD_FACETEDNAVIG_001.detect: Evaluate product listing or search results pages: identify if the filtering UI offers multiple distinct dimensions (facets) or just basic, single-dimension filters.
UX_PRD_FACETEDNAVIG_001.when_to_apply: Apply faceted navigation when users need to narrow down extremely large content sets across multiple distinct dimensions (e.g., e-commerce product catalogs with size, color, brand).
UX_PRD_FACETEDNAVIG_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use faceted navigation if the content set is small or users only need one or two basic criteria, as it adds unnecessary cognitive load and metadata maintenance.
UX_PRD_FACETEDNAVIG_001.quote: The extra power of faceted navigation also adds interaction cost by presenting users with more options to comprehend and manipulate. A simple filter can often be easier to understand and faster to use.

UX_COG_PROGRESSIVED_001.title: Progressive Disclosure
UX_COG_PROGRESSIVED_001.rule: Initially show users only the most important options or content, deferring advanced features or detailed information to secondary screens or expandable sections (like accordions) accessible upon request. Expose all content at once if users need to consume most of it to complete their task.
UX_COG_PROGRESSIVED_001.detect: Identify complex forms, menus, or content-heavy pages. Check if all options or content are presented at once, or if advanced settings and secondary details are hidden behind 'Advanced', 'More options', or accordions. Evaluate if the user task requires accessing most of the hidden information.
UX_COG_PROGRESSIVED_001.when_to_apply: Apply when an interface has a large number of features or dense content, but most users only need a small core subset or a few key pieces of information to complete their primary tasks. Also useful on mobile devices where screen space is limited.
UX_COG_PROGRESSIVED_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to frequently used core features, when users need to consume most or all of the content to answer their questions, when printing the full content is common, or when users must frequently alternate between interdependent options.
UX_COG_PROGRESSIVED_001.quote: Initially, show users only a few of the most important options. Offer a larger set of specialized options upon request.

UX_COG_MILLERSLAW_001.title: Miller's Law
UX_COG_MILLERSLAW_001.rule: Organize content into smaller chunks to reduce cognitive load, rather than strictly limiting interface elements to seven items.
UX_COG_MILLERSLAW_001.detect: Identify flat lists, menus, or data inputs with more than 5-9 un-grouped items, or long unbroken strings of text and numbers.
UX_COG_MILLERSLAW_001.when_to_apply: When presenting complex information, long forms, or data that users need to process, understand, or hold in short-term memory.
UX_COG_MILLERSLAW_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use the 'magical number seven' to justify unnecessary design limitations, such as artificially restricting broad navigation menus where scanning is preferred over memorization.
UX_COG_MILLERSLAW_001.quote: Organize content into smaller chunks to help users process, understand, and memorize easily.

UX_COG_RECOGNITIONO_001.title: Promote Recognition Over Recall
UX_COG_RECOGNITIONO_001.rule: Design interfaces to rely on recognition rather than recall by making information, options, and interface functions visible and easily accessible.
UX_COG_RECOGNITIONO_001.detect: Identify interactions that require users to generate answers from scratch, remember hidden gestures, or memorize upfront tutorials instead of selecting from visible options.
UX_COG_RECOGNITIONO_001.when_to_apply: Apply to menus, search interfaces (via suggestions), task resumption (via history or recently viewed), and complex formatting tasks where users need to select from available commands.
UX_COG_RECOGNITIONO_001.when_not_to_apply: When security necessitates recall (e.g., passwords) or when designing for extreme power users where command-line speed is prioritized over learnability.
UX_COG_RECOGNITIONO_001.quote: How do you promote recognition? By making information and interface functions visible and easily accessible.

UX_COG_OFFLOADCOGNI_001.title: Offload Cognitive Tasks to the System
UX_COG_OFFLOADCOGNI_001.rule: Minimize extraneous cognitive load by offloading tasks from the user to the system. Re-display previously entered information, set smart defaults, and use familiar layouts to reduce the need for users to remember information or make unnecessary decisions.
UX_COG_OFFLOADCOGNI_001.detect: Identify interfaces where users must recall information from previous steps, manually enter standard data, or parse dense text instead of visual cues.
UX_COG_OFFLOADCOGNI_001.when_to_apply: When designing multi-step processes, forms, or complex transactional interfaces where users have specific constraints or goals.
UX_COG_OFFLOADCOGNI_001.when_not_to_apply: When cognitive friction is intentional (e.g., confirming a destructive action) or in educational contexts where intrinsic cognitive load is necessary for learning.
UX_COG_OFFLOADCOGNI_001.quote: Look for anything in your design that requires users to read text, remember information, or make a decision. Then look for alternatives: can you show a picture, re-display previously entered information, or set a smart default?

UX_COG_SERIALPOSITI_001.title: Serial Position Effect
UX_COG_SERIALPOSITI_001.rule: Place the most important items or key actions at the beginning and end of a list or navigation sequence, relegating the least important items to the middle.
UX_COG_SERIALPOSITI_001.detect: Analyze navigation bars, menus, and lists. Verify that primary actions are positioned at the far left or far right, rather than in the middle.
UX_COG_SERIALPOSITI_001.when_to_apply: Apply to navigation menus, feature lists, and action bars where specific items require higher user recall and engagement.
UX_COG_SERIALPOSITI_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when the list requires a strict chronological, alphabetical, or sequential logical order that supersedes priority.
UX_COG_SERIALPOSITI_001.quote: Users have a propensity to best remember the first and last items in a series.

UX_COG_MEGAMENUS_001.title: Use Mega Menus for Large Navigation Sets
UX_COG_MEGAMENUS_001.rule: Use mega menus instead of standard scrolling dropdowns for large navigation sets. Group options logically to allow users to see all choices at a glance, reducing reliance on short-term memory.
UX_COG_MEGAMENUS_001.detect: Identify standard single-column dropdowns that require scrolling to view all navigation options, or mega menus that lack clear visual grouping.
UX_COG_MEGAMENUS_001.when_to_apply: When a site has a large number of navigation options or multiple levels of information architecture that would otherwise require scrolling in a standard dropdown.
UX_COG_MEGAMENUS_001.when_not_to_apply: When the site has a shallow information architecture with few options, or when the menu would require embedding complex GUI widgets like search boxes.
UX_COG_MEGAMENUS_001.quote: Mega menus show everything at a glance, so users can see rather than try to remember. People have enough on their minds, and messing with short-term memory reduces their ability to accomplish tasks.

UX_DS_12STEPCOLORS_001.title: 12-Step Semantic Color Token Scale
UX_DS_12STEPCOLORS_001.rule: Structure tokenized color scales into 12 steps with specific semantic purposes: steps 1-2 for backgrounds, 3-5 for interactive component states, 6-8 for borders and separators, 9-10 for solid backgrounds/brand colors, and 11-12 for accessible text.
UX_DS_12STEPCOLORS_001.detect: Check color token definitions and usage. Verify if scales are divided into 12 steps and if components map their backgrounds, borders, and text to the corresponding semantic steps (e.g., text uses step 11 or 12).
UX_DS_12STEPCOLORS_001.when_to_apply: When designing a comprehensive, accessible design token system for a component library or complex application requiring consistent interactive states and contrast.
UX_DS_12STEPCOLORS_001.when_not_to_apply: When building a simple, single-theme site with minimal interactive states, or when constrained by a legacy 100-900 lightness-based color system.
UX_DS_12STEPCOLORS_001.quote: Each accent is a 12-step scale... /* Backgrounds */ var(--accent-1); var(--accent-2); /* Interactive components */ var(--accent-3); ... /* Borders and separators */ var(--accent-6); ... /* Solid colors */ var(--accent-9); ... /* Accessible text */ var(--accent-11);

UX_DS_CONSISTENCYA_001.title: Opinionated Design Tokens for UI Consistency
UX_DS_CONSISTENCYA_001.rule: Implement design tokens and foundational visual styles (color, spacing, typography) as opinionated building blocks to enforce consistent patterns and components across the interface, ensuring users do not have to relearn how the system works.
UX_DS_CONSISTENCYA_001.detect: Analyze styling code for hardcoded hex codes, absolute pixel values, or custom font definitions instead of standardized design token references. Audit the UI for shared component usage and consistent terminology.
UX_DS_CONSISTENCYA_001.when_to_apply: When building complex platforms, enterprise software, or scalable applications where users perform repeated workflows and rely on predictability and brand consistency.
UX_DS_CONSISTENCYA_001.when_not_to_apply: When designing isolated marketing campaigns, experimental prototypes, or highly specialized tools that explicitly require diverging from the core design system.
UX_DS_CONSISTENCYA_001.quote: Create engaging user experiences with foundations. These include our tokens, guidelines, and visual styles: color, spacing, typography, and more.

UX_INX_CONSTRUCTIVE_001.title: Constructive Error Feedback
UX_INX_CONSTRUCTIVE_001.rule: Express error messages in plain, non-blaming language, precisely indicate the problem, constructively suggest a solution, and display the message adjacent to the affected interface element.
UX_INX_CONSTRUCTIVE_001.detect: Trigger an error state (e.g., invalid form input). Verify that the error message appears in close proximity to the source, avoids technical jargon or user blame, clearly states the issue, and offers an actionable recovery path.
UX_INX_CONSTRUCTIVE_001.when_to_apply: Whenever the system encounters an error, invalid input, or failure state that prevents the user from completing their task, particularly when related to specific interface elements.
UX_INX_CONSTRUCTIVE_001.when_not_to_apply: When the error is purely internal and automatically recoverable (fail silently), or when it is a global system failure unrelated to a specific field (use a global banner instead).
UX_INX_CONSTRUCTIVE_001.quote: Error messages should be expressed in plain language (no error codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.

UX_INX_VISIBILITYOF_001.title: Visibility of System Status
UX_INX_VISIBILITYOF_001.rule: Keep users informed about the current system state, ongoing processes, and successful background operations through appropriate, timely, and explicit feedback to build trust and guide next steps.
UX_INX_VISIBILITYOF_001.detect: Trigger system actions (e.g., form submissions, data loading) or observe idle background processes to verify the presence of immediate visual or textual feedback, progress indicators, or explicit positive status indicators (e.g., 'connected' or 'protected').
UX_INX_VISIBILITYOF_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all interactive elements, asynchronous processes, and critical background states (e.g., security monitoring, syncing) to ensure users feel in control and assured of system health.
UX_INX_VISIBILITYOF_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not expose irrelevant backstage technical details, and avoid persistent 'everything is OK' messages in direct-manipulation tools or instantaneous micro-interactions where native physical responses suffice.
UX_INX_VISIBILITYOF_001.quote: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.

UX_INX_RESPONSETIME_001.title: Response Time Limits and Feedback Thresholds
UX_INX_RESPONSETIME_001.rule: Provide UI feedback based on interaction latency: aim for <100-200ms for an instantaneous feel, <400ms to maintain productivity, >1s requires a busy indicator, and >10s requires a determinate progress bar and a cancel option.
UX_INX_RESPONSETIME_001.detect: Measure interaction latency (e.g., INP). Flag interactions taking >200-400ms without initial visual feedback, >1s without a busy indicator, and >10s without a determinate progress indicator and cancel button.
UX_INX_RESPONSETIME_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all interactive elements where users trigger operations requiring processing, data fetching, or network requests.
UX_INX_RESPONSETIME_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to continuous gestures (scrolling, zooming) which require stricter latency (<16ms), background tasks, or when artificial delays are purposefully used for security or perceived value (e.g., fraud checks).
UX_INX_RESPONSETIME_001.quote: 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously... 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted... 10 seconds is about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue.

UX_INX_MODALUSAGE_001.title: Modal Usage and Constraints
UX_INX_MODALUSAGE_001.rule: Reserve modal dialogs for critical warnings, irreversible actions, or short, essential tasks. Avoid modals for highly repeatable tasks, complex multi-step flows, non-essential interruptions, or when users must reference obscured background information; use full pages or nonmodal dialogs instead.
UX_INX_MODALUSAGE_001.detect: Identify dialogs that disable the main interface. Flag modals containing multi-step flows, excessive vertical scrolling, non-essential promotions, or tasks requiring users to reference the obscured background context.
UX_INX_MODALUSAGE_001.when_to_apply: When designing critical system feedback, alerts, simple confirmations, or short data entry prompts where capturing undivided user attention is strictly required.
UX_INX_MODALUSAGE_001.when_not_to_apply: For frequent repetitive tasks, complex decision-making, dense data input, non-essential promotions, or when the user must reference the obscured background content to complete their task.
UX_INX_MODALUSAGE_001.quote: Modal dialogs interrupt users and demand an action. They are appropriate when user's attention needs to be directed toward important information. [...] For complex flows with complex choices, consider using a full page instead of a modal.

UX_INX_ERRORVALIDAT_001.title: Defer Error Validation to On-Change or On-Submit
UX_INX_ERRORVALIDAT_001.rule: Trigger form validation errors when the user moves focus away from the input (on change/blur) or upon form submission, rather than providing real-time error feedback while the user is actively typing (on input).
UX_INX_ERRORVALIDAT_001.detect: Check event listeners on form inputs. If 'onInput' or 'keyup' events trigger error state rendering before the user blurs the field, it violates this rule.
UX_INX_ERRORVALIDAT_001.when_to_apply: Standard form fields where users input data (text, email, numbers) and validation requires a complete entry to be accurate.
UX_INX_ERRORVALIDAT_001.when_not_to_apply: When providing positive progressive cues (e.g., password strength), indicating progress, or for extremely strict input requirements where immediate formatting correction is necessary.
UX_INX_ERRORVALIDAT_001.quote: While useful for form fields with very strict input requirements, research has proven real-time validation causes more user errors and takes longer to successfully complete the form.

UX_INX_LOADINGSTATE_001.title: Skeleton Screens vs. Spinners for Perceived Performance
UX_INX_LOADINGSTATE_001.rule: Use skeleton screens for full-page loads taking 2-10 seconds to reduce perceived wait time and cognitive load. Use spinners for single-module loads, and progress bars for loads exceeding 10 seconds. Avoid both for loads under 1 second.
UX_INX_LOADINGSTATE_001.detect: Identify loading states in the UI. Measure expected load times and scope (full page vs. single component).
UX_INX_LOADINGSTATE_001.when_to_apply: Apply skeleton screens for full-page or major view transitions that take between 2 and 10 seconds to load.
UX_INX_LOADINGSTATE_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use for loads under 1 second (causes annoying flashing), loads over 10 seconds (use progress bars), single-component loads (use spinners), or background processes like file uploads.
UX_INX_LOADINGSTATE_001.quote: Spinners are typically best used on a single module, like a video or a card which is on a dashboard. Skeleton screens... are better when the full screen is loading because the wireframe gives users a sense of what the page will look like and, thus, minimizes cognitive load.

UX_INX_NOTIFICATION_001.title: Inline vs. Toast Notifications
UX_INX_NOTIFICATION_001.rule: Use inline notifications for persistent, contextual feedback within a task flow. Use toast notifications for short, time-based, non-modal messages that automatically dismiss.
UX_INX_NOTIFICATION_001.detect: Identify the notification behavior and placement: if it auto-dismisses and floats over the UI (usually top right), it should be a toast. If it persists within the page layout near related content, it should be inline.
UX_INX_NOTIFICATION_001.when_to_apply: Use inline notifications for form errors, task statuses, or when the message must persist until resolved. Use toast notifications for quick, non-critical confirmations (e.g., 'Saved successfully') that do not require user interaction.
UX_INX_NOTIFICATION_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use toast notifications for critical errors or messages requiring user action, as they may disappear before the user reads them. Do not use inline notifications for global, transient system updates.
UX_INX_NOTIFICATION_001.quote: Inline notifications show up in task flows to notify users of the status of an action... Toast notifications are non-modal, time-based window elements used to display short messages; they usually appear at the top of the screen and disappear after a few seconds.

UX_INX_CONSISTENCY_001.title: Maintain Consistent Button Placement Across Multipage Forms
UX_INX_CONSISTENCY_001.rule: Keep primary and secondary action buttons in consistent relative positions across all pages of a multipage form or wizard to prevent accidental actions.
UX_INX_CONSISTENCY_001.detect: Identify multipage forms or wizards. Check the layout of action buttons on each page. Flag if the primary/secondary button order (e.g., left vs. right) changes between steps.
UX_INX_CONSISTENCY_001.when_to_apply: When designing wizards, checkout flows, or any multipage data entry process.
UX_INX_CONSISTENCY_001.when_not_to_apply: When a specific step requires a fundamentally different interaction model, such as a final destructive confirmation step that intentionally disrupts flow to force attention.
UX_INX_CONSISTENCY_001.quote: Ensure consistency in the placement of form fields and buttons, especially for multipage forms or wizards.

UX_INX_ERRORFOCUSMA_001.title: Form Error Banner Focus Management
UX_INX_ERRORFOCUSMA_001.rule: When a user submits a complex form with errors, display a critical summary banner at the top of the form and programmatically move focus to it. Never move focus to banners that appear on initial page load.
UX_INX_ERRORFOCUSMA_001.detect: Identify form submission handlers. If validation fails, verify that a summary alert/banner is rendered at the top of the form, focus is programmatically shifted to this banner, and inline errors are displayed on the specific fields.
UX_INX_ERRORFOCUSMA_001.when_to_apply: When users submit long or complex forms that result in validation errors, requiring a summary of what went wrong to assist workflows for users with disabilities.
UX_INX_ERRORFOCUSMA_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not move focus to banners if they appear on page load, or if they convey information outside the user's current workflow. Avoid for very short, single-input forms where inline errors suffice.
UX_INX_ERRORFOCUSMA_001.quote: When merchants submit long or complex forms with errors, use a critical banner to summarize what went wrong. Place the banner at the top of the form and move focus to the banner when the form is submitted.

UX_INX_ARIALIVEREGI_001.title: Use ARIA Live Regions for Status Updates Without Moving Focus
UX_INX_ARIALIVEREGI_001.rule: Use `aria-live="polite"` or `role="status"` to announce dynamic, non-interactive status updates to assistive technologies without forcing a page reload or moving the user's focus.
UX_INX_ARIALIVEREGI_001.detect: Identify dynamic DOM updates (e.g., search results, toast notifications, status messages) that do not receive focus. Verify they are wrapped in an element with `aria-live="polite"` or `role="status"` present in the DOM before the update occurs.
UX_INX_ARIALIVEREGI_001.when_to_apply: Apply when a part of the page updates dynamically with information useful to the user (e.g., search results loaded, form saved) but doesn't require immediate interaction or focus management.
UX_INX_ARIALIVEREGI_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when the update requires immediate user interaction (move focus instead), or when the update is a critical error that must interrupt the user immediately (use `aria-live="assertive"` or `role="alert"`).
UX_INX_ARIALIVEREGI_001.quote: Using JavaScript, it is possible to dynamically change parts of a page without requiring the entire page to reload... ARIA live regions fill this gap and provide a way to programmatically expose dynamic content changes in a way that can be announced by assistive technologies.

UX_ARC_ARIADESCRIBE_001.title: Associate Form Instructions, Hints, and Errors via aria-describedby
UX_ARC_ARIADESCRIBE_001.rule: Use the aria-describedby attribute on form inputs to programmatically associate them with corresponding inline instructions, hint text, and error messages. Keep associated text concise (e.g., a single short sentence) and avoid interactive elements like links within the description.
UX_ARC_ARIADESCRIBE_001.detect: Identify form inputs with adjacent helper text or error messages. Verify the input has an aria-describedby attribute containing the ID(s) of the descriptive element(s). Check that the described-by elements do not contain complex formatting or interactive tags like <a>.
UX_ARC_ARIADESCRIBE_001.when_to_apply: When a form field has specific formatting requirements, supplementary hint text, cues, or validation error messages located near the input field.
UX_ARC_ARIADESCRIBE_001.when_not_to_apply: When instructions are general and placed at the beginning of the form, when the <label> text already fully encapsulates the instruction, or when the explanation requires complex, multi-sentence formatting or links.
UX_ARC_ARIADESCRIBE_001.quote: Although labels are announced when form inputs received keyboard focus, other text between the form controls is usually skipped. Be sure to include any instructions at the beginning of the form, or associate them with specific fields using aria-describedby.

UX_ARC_TEXTINPUTOVE_001.title: Avoid Dropdowns for Familiar or Easily Typed Data
UX_ARC_TEXTINPUTOVE_001.rule: Use text input fields instead of dropdowns for highly familiar data (like birthdates) or data that is faster to type (like states or countries). Long dropdowns force users to scroll and carefully steer the mouse (violating the Steering Law/Fitts' Law), which degrades form completion speed.
UX_ARC_TEXTINPUTOVE_001.detect: Identify <select> elements in forms used for states, countries, or dates of birth, especially those with many options requiring scrolling.
UX_ARC_TEXTINPUTOVE_001.when_to_apply: Apply to form fields where the user already knows the answer by heart (e.g., DOB) or can type a standard abbreviation quickly (e.g., 'NY' for New York).
UX_ARC_TEXTINPUTOVE_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when the list of valid options is small (under 10 items), highly specific, or unfamiliar to the user, making discovery necessary.
UX_ARC_TEXTINPUTOVE_001.quote: Very long dropdowns that require scrolling make it impossible for users to see all their choices in one glance. They also require careful steering of the mouse so that it does not leave the dropdown. (This is an instance of the steering law... derived from Fitts’ law...)

UX_ARC_AVOIDRESETBU_001.title: Avoid Reset and Clear Buttons
UX_ARC_AVOIDRESETBU_001.rule: Do not include Reset or Clear buttons in web forms to prevent accidental deletion of user input.
UX_ARC_AVOIDRESETBU_001.detect: Identify button elements with type='reset' or text labels containing 'Clear' or 'Reset'.
UX_ARC_AVOIDRESETBU_001.when_to_apply: Apply to standard web forms, data entry screens, and checkout flows.
UX_ARC_AVOIDRESETBU_001.when_not_to_apply: Forms collecting extremely sensitive input where users might explicitly need to abandon and wipe their data, though a visually de-emphasized Cancel button is preferred.
UX_ARC_AVOIDRESETBU_001.quote: The risk of accidental deletion outweighs the unlikely need to 'start over' on a web form.

UX_ARC_RADIOVSCHECK_001.title: Checkbox vs. Radio Button Selection
UX_ARC_RADIOVSCHECK_001.rule: Use radio buttons for mutually exclusive lists where exactly one option must be selected. Use checkboxes when users can select any number of options (zero, one, or multiple).
UX_ARC_RADIOVSCHECK_001.detect: Identify lists of options in forms. Check if mutually exclusive options use checkboxes (violation) or if multi-select options use radio buttons (violation).
UX_ARC_RADIOVSCHECK_001.when_to_apply: When designing forms, settings, or surveys where users must select from a predefined list of options.
UX_ARC_RADIOVSCHECK_001.when_not_to_apply: When options are not predefined, or when the control triggers an immediate action (use action buttons instead).
UX_ARC_RADIOVSCHECK_001.quote: Radio buttons are used when there is a list of two or more options that are mutually exclusive and the user must select exactly one choice. Checkboxes are used when there are lists of options and the user may select any number of choices, including zero, one, or several.

UX_ARC_IMMEDIATEINL_001.title: Immediate Inline Validation Feedback
UX_ARC_IMMEDIATEINL_001.rule: Provide immediate inline validation feedback using client-side scripts or HTML5 constraints to verify data formats and display errors when a user leaves a field (on blur) or during entry, rather than waiting for form submission.
UX_ARC_IMMEDIATEINL_001.detect: Inspect form inputs for constraint validation attributes (e.g., required, pattern, type="email") and verify the presence of 'blur' or 'input' event listeners that trigger inline error messages in the DOM before submission.
UX_ARC_IMMEDIATEINL_001.when_to_apply: When forms require specific data formats, mandatory fields, or constraints (e.g., sign-up, checkout, contact forms), allowing users to correct errors immediately in context.
UX_ARC_IMMEDIATEINL_001.when_not_to_apply: When input is entirely free-form, when validation strictly requires server-side context (e.g., checking username availability), or when aggressive 'input' validation would flag errors before the user finishes typing a valid entry.
UX_ARC_IMMEDIATEINL_001.quote: Error messages should show the message when the user leaves the field and not just at submission. Research demonstrates that even just the timing of the feedback alone significantly disrupts user performance.

UX_ARC_VISIBLELABEL_001.title: Do Not Use Placeholders as Replacements for Field Labels
UX_ARC_VISIBLELABEL_001.rule: Always provide clear, visible labels placed outside empty form fields. Never use in-field placeholder text as the sole label for a form field.
UX_ARC_VISIBLELABEL_001.detect: Check form fields to ensure they have an associated visible label outside the input. Verify that the placeholder attribute is not the only indicator of the field's purpose.
UX_ARC_VISIBLELABEL_001.when_to_apply: When designing any data entry form, to ensure users can remember field requirements, check their work, recover from errors, and navigate accessibly.
UX_ARC_VISIBLELABEL_001.when_not_to_apply: Extremely simple, ubiquitous single-field forms (like a global search box with a magnifying glass icon) where context makes the input purpose universally obvious.
UX_ARC_VISIBLELABEL_001.quote: Rather than risk having users stumble while filling out forms or waste valuable time figuring out how they work, the best solution is to have clear, visible labels that are placed outside empty form fields.

UX_ARC_ERRORSUMMARY_001.title: Form Error Summary Pattern
UX_ARC_ERRORSUMMARY_001.rule: Display an error summary at the top of the page on validation failure, move keyboard focus to it, and include links to the specific fields with errors. Ensure the summary text exactly matches the inline error messages.
UX_ARC_ERRORSUMMARY_001.detect: Trigger a form validation error. Verify an error summary appears at the top of the <main> container, focus shifts to it, and it contains anchor links pointing to the corresponding invalid input fields.
UX_ARC_ERRORSUMMARY_001.when_to_apply: Always show an error summary when there is a form validation error upon submission, even if there is only a single error.
UX_ARC_ERRORSUMMARY_001.when_not_to_apply: When validation is purely preventative (e.g., blocking invalid characters on keypress) without triggering a form-level submission error state.
UX_ARC_ERRORSUMMARY_001.quote: When a user makes an error, you must show both an error summary and an Error message component next to each answer that contains an error... move keyboard focus to the error summary... link to each of the answers that have validation errors

UX_ARC_FIELDSETLEGE_001.title: Group Related Inputs with Fieldset and Legend
UX_ARC_FIELDSETLEGE_001.rule: Group related form inputs (such as radio buttons, checkboxes, or multi-part fields like addresses and dates) within a <fieldset> element. The first child of the <fieldset> must be a <legend> that describes the group or asks the question. If the group is the sole question on the page, set the <legend> as the page heading (e.g., containing an <h1>).
UX_ARC_FIELDSETLEGE_001.detect: Identify related inputs (e.g., radios or checkboxes sharing a name attribute, or clustered fields like dates). Verify they are enclosed in a <fieldset> and that the first child is a <legend>. If it is the only form control on the page, check if the <legend> contains an <h1>.
