UX_ARC_FIELDSETLEGE_001.when_to_apply: When presenting mutually exclusive radio buttons, multiple related checkboxes, or a cohesive group of inputs (like an address) that require shared context to be fully understood.
UX_ARC_FIELDSETLEGE_001.when_not_to_apply: When a single form control is used (e.g., a standalone text input or a single boolean checkbox for 'I agree to terms') where the individual <label> provides sufficient context.
UX_ARC_FIELDSETLEGE_001.quote: Use the fieldset component when you need to show a relationship between multiple form inputs.

UX_ARC_ACCESSIBLETO_001.title: Inclusive Toggle Button Pattern
UX_ARC_ACCESSIBLETO_001.rule: Implement toggle buttons using `<button>` elements with `aria-pressed` or `role="switch"` and `aria-checked`. Never change the text label (e.g., 'Play' to 'Pause') and the ARIA state simultaneously.
UX_ARC_ACCESSIBLETO_001.detect: Check if a toggle control uses a `<button>` element with `aria-pressed` or `role="switch"` + `aria-checked`. Verify via DOM mutation observers or code inspection that the button's text content and its ARIA state attribute do not toggle at the same time.
UX_ARC_ACCESSIBLETO_001.when_to_apply: When creating custom on/off switches or toggle buttons that change interface state instantaneously without submitting form data.
UX_ARC_ACCESSIBLETO_001.when_not_to_apply: When the control is part of a standard form data collection process, where native `<input type="checkbox">` or `<input type="radio">` are more appropriate and expected by users.
UX_ARC_ACCESSIBLETO_001.quote: As a rule of thumb, you should never change pressed state and label together. If the label changes, the button has already changed state in a sense, just not via explicit WAI-ARIA state management.

UX_ARC_CONSTRAINTVA_001.title: Integrate Custom Form Validation via setCustomValidity()
UX_ARC_CONSTRAINTVA_001.rule: Use the Constraint Validation API's setCustomValidity() method to enforce complex form constraints (e.g., cross-field checks, file size limits) while maintaining native browser validation UI. Pass an empty string to mark the field as valid, or a descriptive error message to mark it as invalid and display the message to the user.
UX_ARC_CONSTRAINTVA_001.detect: Look for custom form validation logic that manually manipulates DOM error messages and prevents submission via event.preventDefault(), instead of leveraging HTMLInputElement.setCustomValidity().
UX_ARC_CONSTRAINTVA_001.when_to_apply: When standard HTML attributes (pattern, min, max) are insufficient for the validation logic (e.g., checking file sizes, comparing two password fields) but you still want to use native :valid/:invalid CSS and browser error popups.
UX_ARC_CONSTRAINTVA_001.when_not_to_apply: When implementing a completely custom form validation UI that intentionally bypasses native browser tooltips (often using the novalidate attribute on the form).
UX_ARC_CONSTRAINTVA_001.quote: With inline validation, users have to repeatedly switch between two quite different mental modes: form-filling and error-correcting... It’s best to keep the validation message until the user has finished with an input field and moved on to the next.

UX_ARC_MARKMINORITY_001.title: Mark Only the Minority Field Requirement Status
UX_ARC_MARKMINORITY_001.rule: Evaluate the overall proportion of required vs. optional fields in a form. If the majority are required, mark only the optional fields with '(optional)'. If the majority are optional, mark only the required fields with '(required)'.
UX_ARC_MARKMINORITY_001.detect: Count the number of required and optional fields in a form. Verify that only the minority status is explicitly labeled to prevent visual clutter.
UX_ARC_MARKMINORITY_001.when_to_apply: When designing forms with a mix of required and optional fields, to reduce visual noise.
UX_ARC_MARKMINORITY_001.when_not_to_apply: When strict legal or specific accessibility compliance mandates explicit marking of all required fields regardless of proportion.
UX_ARC_MARKMINORITY_001.quote: If the majority of the fields are required, mark only the optional field labels with (optional). If the majority of the fields are optional, mark only the required field labels with (required).

UX_ARC_INLINEERRORM_001.title: Per-Field Error Message Pattern
UX_ARC_INLINEERRORM_001.rule: Display validation error messages directly above the affected input (after the label and hint text) in red, apply a red border to the input field, prepend a visually hidden 'Error:' prefix for screen readers, and preserve the user's invalid input.
UX_ARC_INLINEERRORM_001.detect: Trigger a form validation error. Verify the error text appears between the label/hint and the input field, the input has a red border, the original input value is retained, and a visually hidden 'Error:' span precedes the message text.
UX_ARC_INLINEERRORM_001.when_to_apply: When a user submits a form containing field-level validation errors.
UX_ARC_INLINEERRORM_001.when_not_to_apply: When the error is a system failure, lack of capacity, or eligibility issue rather than a correctable user input error.
UX_ARC_INLINEERRORM_001.quote: For each error: put the message in red after the question text and hint text... use a red border to visually connect the message and the question it belongs to... Do not clear any form fields when showing the Error message component.

UX_ARC_POSTELSLAW_001.title: Postel's Law (Robustness Principle)
UX_ARC_POSTELSLAW_001.rule: Accept variable input from users and translate it to meet system requirements rather than forcing strict formatting.
UX_ARC_POSTELSLAW_001.detect: Identify form inputs (e.g., phone numbers, dates, credit cards) that throw validation errors for common formatting variations like spaces or dashes instead of auto-cleaning the data.
UX_ARC_POSTELSLAW_001.when_to_apply: When designing forms and data entry fields where human input naturally varies in format (e.g., phone numbers, currency, dates).
UX_ARC_POSTELSLAW_001.when_not_to_apply: When strict input validation is required for security reasons (e.g., passwords, cryptographic keys) or when ambiguous input could lead to destructive actions.
UX_ARC_POSTELSLAW_001.quote: Accept variable input from users, translating that input to meet your requirements, defining boundaries for input, and providing clear feedback to the user.

UX_ARC_PASSWORDVISI_001.title: Provide Clear-Text Password Visibility
UX_ARC_PASSWORDVISI_001.rule: Allow users to see the passwords they are typing by providing a show password toggle, or default to clear text for low-risk applications.
UX_ARC_PASSWORDVISI_001.detect: Identify input[type="password"] fields and check for an associated toggle control that changes the input type to text.
UX_ARC_PASSWORDVISI_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all login and registration forms, particularly on mobile devices where typing is difficult and error-prone.
UX_ARC_PASSWORDVISI_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not default to clear text for high-risk applications like banking, though a user-activated toggle should still be provided.
UX_ARC_PASSWORDVISI_001.quote: When you make it hard for users to enter passwords you create two problems... Users make more errors when they can't see what they're typing.

UX_ARC_MULTISTEPFOR_001.title: Use Multi-Step Layouts for Long Forms
UX_ARC_MULTISTEPFOR_001.rule: Split long forms into multiple steps (2-3 steps) and place sensitive fields (like email or phone) on the final step to reduce initial intimidation and leverage the sunk cost fallacy.
UX_ARC_MULTISTEPFOR_001.detect: Single-page forms with many fields (>6) or forms asking for sensitive contact information upfront alongside other data.
UX_ARC_MULTISTEPFOR_001.when_to_apply: When designing lead generation, onboarding, or complex data-entry forms that require significant user effort.
UX_ARC_MULTISTEPFOR_001.when_not_to_apply: When the form is already very short (1-3 fields), such as a simple login or newsletter signup.
UX_ARC_MULTISTEPFOR_001.quote: Splitting your forms into two or three steps will almost always increase form completion... By asking for sensitive information (email, phone) on the final step of a multi-step form, users are more likely to fill out these fields

UX_GEN_JAKOBSLAW_001.title: Jakob's Law
UX_GEN_JAKOBSLAW_001.rule: Design interfaces that conform to users' pre-existing mental models by leveraging established industry conventions, allowing users to focus on tasks rather than learning new interaction styles.
UX_GEN_JAKOBSLAW_001.detect: Identify non-standard UI patterns for common tasks (e.g., custom form controls, unconventional navigation placement, unexpected e-commerce flows) that deviate from standard web conventions and force users to learn a new mental model.
UX_GEN_JAKOBSLAW_001.when_to_apply: When designing core navigation, standard UI components, common workflows (like shopping carts), search functionalities, and basic controls where industry conventions are well-established.
UX_GEN_JAKOBSLAW_001.when_not_to_apply: When a new interaction paradigm is demonstrably superior, thoroughly tested, provides massive efficiency gains, or when existing mental models do not apply (accompanied by sufficient onboarding).
UX_GEN_JAKOBSLAW_001.quote: Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.

UX_GEN_DOHERTYTHRES_001.title: Doherty Threshold
UX_GEN_DOHERTYTHRES_001.rule: Keep system response times under 400ms to ensure users do not have to wait on the computer, maintaining their productivity and flow.
UX_GEN_DOHERTYTHRES_001.detect: Measure the time between user input (e.g., click, tap) and the corresponding UI feedback. Flag any interactions that exceed 400 milliseconds.
UX_GEN_DOHERTYTHRES_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all standard UI interactions, page navigations, and state changes to maintain a seamless user experience.
UX_GEN_DOHERTYTHRES_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when a deliberate delay is required for security (e.g., login throttling) or to build trust by showing the system is 'working hard' on a complex task.
UX_GEN_DOHERTYTHRES_001.quote: Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (<400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other.

UX_GEN_RESPONSIVEWE_001.title: Responsive Web Design Foundations
UX_GEN_RESPONSIVEWE_001.rule: Use fluid grids, flexible images, and media queries to create a single, adaptive layout that responds to the user's viewport, rather than building separate device-specific experiences.
UX_GEN_RESPONSIVEWE_001.detect: Identify fixed-width containers that overflow on small screens, or the presence of device-specific redirects (e.g., m.domain.com) instead of CSS media queries.
UX_GEN_RESPONSIVEWE_001.when_to_apply: When building web interfaces that will be accessed across a gradient of different devices, screen sizes, and resolutions.
UX_GEN_RESPONSIVEWE_001.when_not_to_apply: When the user goals for a specific device (like mobile) are drastically limited or different in scope, making a separate, highly tailored application more appropriate.
UX_GEN_RESPONSIVEWE_001.quote: Rather than tailoring disconnected designs to each of an ever-increasing number of web devices, we can treat them as facets of the same experience.

UX_GEN_NIELSENSUSAB_001.title: The Five Components of Usability
UX_GEN_NIELSENSUSAB_001.rule: Evaluate user interfaces against the five core components of usability: learnability (first-time ease), efficiency (speed after learning), memorability (ease of returning), errors (frequency, severity, and recovery), and satisfaction (pleasantness).
UX_GEN_NIELSENSUSAB_001.detect: Check if usability evaluations and metrics explicitly account for learnability, efficiency, memorability, error rates, and user satisfaction, rather than just binary task success.
UX_GEN_NIELSENSUSAB_001.when_to_apply: When defining usability metrics, planning user tests, or evaluating the overall quality of a user interface.
UX_GEN_NIELSENSUSAB_001.when_not_to_apply: When evaluating pure utility (whether the system has the required features) or underlying technical performance independent of the user interface.
UX_GEN_NIELSENSUSAB_001.quote: Usability is defined by 5 quality components: Learnability... Efficiency... Memorability... Errors... Satisfaction...

UX_VIS_VISUALHIERAR_001.title: Establish Clear Visual Hierarchy
UX_VIS_VISUALHIERAR_001.rule: Establish a clear visual hierarchy by varying scale, color, contrast, and whitespace to rank UI components. Avoid giving all elements equal visual weight, as it creates visual clutter and prevents users from knowing where to focus.
UX_VIS_VISUALHIERAR_001.detect: Identify interfaces where multiple key elements (KPIs, CTAs, content blocks) share uniform size, color saturation, and spacing, resulting in no clear focal point or scanning order.
UX_VIS_VISUALHIERAR_001.when_to_apply: When designing dashboards, landing pages, or complex layouts containing multiple pieces of information or actions with varying levels of importance that users need to scan and process in a specific order.
UX_VIS_VISUALHIERAR_001.when_not_to_apply: When displaying a uniform collection of items that genuinely share the exact same priority, such as a standard data table or a homogeneous product grid, where uniform spacing and weight are needed to group by similarity.
UX_VIS_VISUALHIERAR_001.quote: If everything is contrasted, then nothing stands out.

UX_VIS_GESTALTPRINC_001.title: Apply Gestalt Principles for Visual Grouping
UX_VIS_GESTALTPRINC_001.rule: Leverage the five Gestalt principles (Proximity, Similarity, Continuity, Closure, Connectedness) to organize UI elements into predictable groups, reducing visual clutter and establishing clear hierarchy without relying solely on explicit borders.
UX_VIS_GESTALTPRINC_001.detect: Evaluate if related elements are grouped using whitespace (proximity), shared visual traits (similarity), or connecting lines (connectedness) rather than relying exclusively on heavy borders or explicit containers.
UX_VIS_GESTALTPRINC_001.when_to_apply: Apply when organizing complex layouts, forms, or data-dense screens to help users quickly parse relationships and navigate the interface intuitively.
UX_VIS_GESTALTPRINC_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not rely solely on subtle Gestalt cues if strict, unambiguous separation is required for legal, security, or severe accessibility constraints where explicit borders are necessary.
UX_VIS_GESTALTPRINC_001.quote: They state that our minds have a tendency to group and organize elements and do so in predictable ways.

UX_VIS_LAWOFPRAGNAN_001.title: Apply Prägnanz to Reduce Visual Density
UX_VIS_LAWOFPRAGNAN_001.rule: Leverage the Gestalt principle of Prägnanz (conciseness) by maximizing negative space and removing non-essential embellishments to reduce visual density and cognitive load.
UX_VIS_LAWOFPRAGNAN_001.detect: Evaluate the interface for unnecessary decorative elements, excessive text, or a lack of negative space around key focal points.
UX_VIS_LAWOFPRAGNAN_001.when_to_apply: When designing complex interfaces where users need to quickly identify core messages or actions without being overwhelmed by information overload.
UX_VIS_LAWOFPRAGNAN_001.when_not_to_apply: When designing data-dense analytical tools (like dashboards or spreadsheets) where high information density is explicitly required by expert users.
UX_VIS_LAWOFPRAGNAN_001.quote: The principle of Prägnanz ("conciseness") is a key tenet of Gestalt psychology that states that the human brain tends to perceive visual stimuli in the simplest way possible. This implies that designs should be kept as uncluttered and streamlined as possible, without any unnecessary elements that might distract from the core message.

UX_VIS_LAWOFSIMILAR_001.title: Gestalt Similarity for Control Grouping
UX_VIS_LAWOFSIMILAR_001.rule: Group related UI controls and signify common functionality by applying shared visual characteristics—such as color, shape, or size—while intentionally varying these traits for unrelated or differing actions.
UX_VIS_LAWOFSIMILAR_001.detect: Identify sets of controls or interactive elements. Verify that elements with similar functions share a distinct visual trait (e.g., color or shape) and that decorative or unrelated elements do not mimic these interactive traits.
UX_VIS_LAWOFSIMILAR_001.when_to_apply: When designing navigation, forms, or toolbars where users need to quickly scan and identify elements that perform similar functions or belong to the same category.
UX_VIS_LAWOFSIMILAR_001.when_not_to_apply: When elements are fundamentally different in function, importance, or interactivity (e.g., primary vs. secondary buttons, interactive buttons vs. decorative icons).
UX_VIS_LAWOFSIMILAR_001.quote: The principle of similarity simply states that when items share some visual characteristic, they are assumed to be related in some way.

UX_VIS_VONRESTORFFE_001.title: Isolation Effect for Primary CTA Emphasis
UX_VIS_VONRESTORFFE_001.rule: Make primary key actions visually distinctive from surrounding elements to ensure they are easily identified and remembered, while exercising restraint to prevent visual competition.
UX_VIS_VONRESTORFFE_001.detect: Check if the primary CTA has a unique visual treatment (e.g., contrasting background color, size, or shape) compared to secondary buttons or surrounding elements, without relying solely on color.
UX_VIS_VONRESTORFFE_001.when_to_apply: When there is a clear primary action or critical information that users need to find and remember among a group of similar items.
UX_VIS_VONRESTORFFE_001.when_not_to_apply: When all actions have equal priority, or when overusing emphasis would cause visual competition and make elements look like advertisements.
UX_VIS_VONRESTORFFE_001.quote: The Von Restorff effect, also known as The Isolation Effect, predicts that when multiple similar objects are present, the one that differs from the rest is most likely to be remembered.

UX_VIS_PROGRESSIVED_001.title: Limit Density in Expandable Data Table Rows
UX_VIS_PROGRESSIVED_001.rule: Use expandable rows for supplementary information, but if the expanded content becomes cramped or overly complex, move the information to a dedicated page, side panel, or separate data table.
UX_VIS_PROGRESSIVED_001.detect: A data table uses expandable rows containing complex layouts, nested tables, or dense forms.
UX_VIS_PROGRESSIVED_001.when_to_apply: When designing data tables that require progressive disclosure of supplementary row details.
UX_VIS_PROGRESSIVED_001.when_not_to_apply: When the supplementary data is simple (e.g., a few text fields) and fits comfortably within the expanded row without scrolling or complex interactions.
UX_VIS_PROGRESSIVED_001.quote: When the content in the expanded area feels cramped, consider taking the user to a dedicated page, side panel, or data table to view the information and complete tasks.

UX_VIS_CARDSVSLISTS_001.title: Use Cards for Heterogeneous Browsing, Lists for Homogeneous Scanning
UX_VIS_CARDSVSLISTS_001.rule: Use card layouts to group heterogeneous content types for browsing, but use standard vertical lists for homogeneous items to support scannability, comparison, and higher information density.
UX_VIS_CARDSVSLISTS_001.detect: Identify repeating item layouts. Check if space-consuming cards (with borders/shadows) are used for highly homogeneous data where users need to scan or compare attributes, rather than using a dense vertical list.
UX_VIS_CARDSVSLISTS_001.when_to_apply: Apply card layouts when displaying dashboards, social feeds, or aggregation sites containing a variety of content types (heterogeneous items) where users are casually browsing rather than searching.
UX_VIS_CARDSVSLISTS_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use cards when users need to search for a specific item, compare multiple options (like pricing or specs), or view highly homogeneous content.
UX_VIS_CARDSVSLISTS_001.quote: Cards work best for collections of heterogeneous items... When presenting very homogenous items... consider using a standard vertical list of items... instead of cards to support scannability and also comparisons among items.

UX_VIS_LAYOUTPRIMIT_001.title: Use Layout Primitives for Spacing and Alignment
UX_VIS_LAYOUTPRIMIT_001.rule: Handle all layouts and spacing using dedicated layout primitives (e.g., Box, Block stack, Inline stack, Grid) rather than embedding custom CSS margins, padding, or flex/grid properties within feature components.
UX_VIS_LAYOUTPRIMIT_001.detect: Scan for custom CSS classes, inline styles, or styled-components applying 'margin', 'padding', 'display: flex', or 'display: grid' in feature components instead of using imported layout primitive components.
UX_VIS_LAYOUTPRIMIT_001.when_to_apply: When arranging elements on a page, managing spacing between components, or building responsive layouts within a design system that provides layout primitives.
UX_VIS_LAYOUTPRIMIT_001.when_not_to_apply: When building the foundational layout primitives themselves, or when working in a legacy codebase without a standardized set of layout components.
UX_VIS_LAYOUTPRIMIT_001.quote: All layouts and spacing should be handled using layout primitives. This keeps our components simple, flexible and composable.

UX_VIS_STICKYNAVIGA_001.title: Evaluate Sticky Header Utility vs. Screen Real Estate
UX_VIS_STICKYNAVIGA_001.rule: Implement sticky headers only if navigation elements are frequently needed mid-scroll. To prevent obscuring focus, maximize the content-to-chrome ratio, ensure high contrast with an opaque background, and avoid distracting animations.
UX_VIS_STICKYNAVIGA_001.detect: Identify sticky headers on scroll. Measure the vertical height consumed (content-to-chrome ratio), check for background opacity, and assess if the persistent elements (e.g., login, search, main nav) are contextually required mid-page.
UX_VIS_STICKYNAVIGA_001.when_to_apply: Apply when users frequently jump between categories, use search, or access utility navigation (like a shopping cart) from deep within a scrolling page.
UX_VIS_STICKYNAVIGA_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply when users typically consume content linearly without needing to navigate away, or when the header elements are rarely used mid-session.
UX_VIS_STICKYNAVIGA_001.quote: Sticky headers can be a positive addition to a site, but only if they truly serve a purpose for your users. If a sticky header does provide value to users, then ensure that it is as small as reasonably possible, it has high contrast against the background, does not use gratuitous animation, does not obscure content, and does not distract your users.

UX_HFE_USABILITYQUE_001.title: Select the Right Usability Questionnaire (SUS, SEQ, NASA-TLX)
UX_HFE_USABILITYQUE_001.rule: Use the System Usability Scale (SUS) post-test to measure overall perceived usability, the Single Ease Question (SEQ) post-task to measure specific task difficulty, and the NASA-TLX post-task to measure workload in complex, mission-critical systems.
UX_HFE_USABILITYQUE_001.detect: Review usability test protocols to ensure SUS is administered at the end of the session, while SEQ or NASA-TLX are administered immediately after individual tasks.
UX_HFE_USABILITYQUE_001.when_to_apply: When conducting summative quantitative studies (n >= 20-30) to benchmark usability, compare design iterations, or identify problematic workflows using standardized, validated instruments.
UX_HFE_USABILITYQUE_001.when_not_to_apply: When conducting small-sample qualitative studies (e.g., 5 users) where numeric scores lack statistical significance, unless explicitly paired with qualitative follow-up questions (e.g., 'Why did you give this score?').
UX_HFE_USABILITYQUE_001.quote: In most cases, use the SUS after the test and the SEQ after each task, as satisfaction metrics to complement other performance metrics... If you have the special case of complex, mission-critical workflows, replace the SEQ with NASA-TLX.

UX_HCI_TOUCHTARGETS_001.title: Minimum Touch Target Size
UX_HCI_TOUCHTARGETS_001.rule: Interactive elements on touchscreens must have a minimum physical rendered size of 1cm x 1cm (0.4in x 0.4in) or adhere to standard design system sizing tokens (e.g., 44px/48px) to ensure accurate selection and prevent accidental taps.
UX_HCI_TOUCHTARGETS_001.detect: Measure the physical rendered dimensions or inspect CSS for standard sizing tokens on interactive elements. Verify that both height and width meet the minimum threshold (e.g., 1cm or 44px/48px) and are not hardcoded to smaller, non-compliant pixel values.
UX_HCI_TOUCHTARGETS_001.when_to_apply: Apply to all interactive elements (buttons, links, icons) on touchscreen interfaces, or when adopting a token-based design system for consistent hit areas.
UX_HCI_TOUCHTARGETS_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to non-interactive, purely decorative elements, or strictly to mouse-driven desktop interfaces. Do not limit to the minimum size when the context involves movement or specific audiences (e.g., children, seniors) requiring even larger targets.
UX_HCI_TOUCHTARGETS_001.quote: Interactive elements must be at least 1cm × 1cm (0.4in × 0.4in) to support adequate selection time and prevent fat-finger errors.

UX_HCI_DOUBLECLICKP_001.title: Prevent Accidental Double-Clicks on Submit Buttons
UX_HCI_DOUBLECLICKP_001.rule: Implement double-click prevention on form submit buttons to protect users with motor impairments (e.g., hand tremors) from accidentally submitting information multiple times.
UX_HCI_DOUBLECLICKP_001.detect: Inspect form submit buttons for debounce logic, immediate disabled states upon click, or specific attributes like `data-prevent-double-click`.
UX_HCI_DOUBLECLICKP_001.when_to_apply: Apply to form submission buttons where duplicate submissions would cause errors, duplicate records, or trigger multiple irreversible actions (e.g., sending emails, processing payments).
UX_HCI_DOUBLECLICKP_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to standard navigation links or buttons that do not trigger state changes or data submission.
UX_HCI_DOUBLECLICKP_001.quote: Sometimes, users double click buttons because they... have motor impairments such as hand tremors which cause them to click the button involuntarily... you can configure the button to ignore the second click.

UX_HCI_UNIFORMBUTTO_001.title: Uniform Width for Button Groups
UX_HCI_UNIFORMBUTTO_001.rule: Apply the same width to all related buttons in a group (excluding ghost buttons), typically matching the width of the button with the longest label.
UX_HCI_UNIFORMBUTTO_001.detect: Identify adjacent buttons within a button group container (e.g., primary and secondary pairs). Measure their rendered widths and flag if the widths are not equal.
UX_HCI_UNIFORMBUTTO_001.when_to_apply: When placing multiple related buttons next to each other in forms, dialogs, or standard layouts to improve visual rhythm and provide predictable hit targets.
UX_HCI_UNIFORMBUTTO_001.when_not_to_apply: When using ghost buttons, icon-only buttons, or when buttons are fluidly spanning a container as a percentage (e.g., 50% each in a narrow mobile view).
UX_HCI_UNIFORMBUTTO_001.quote: When using groups of related buttons (not including ghost buttons), they should all be the same width. The width of all the buttons is usually determined by the longest button label.

UX_PRD_PEAKENDRULE_001.title: Peak-End Rule for Onboarding Flows
UX_PRD_PEAKENDRULE_001.rule: Optimize the emotional peak and the final step of onboarding flows to be highly positive and rewarding, as users judge the overall experience based on these specific moments rather than the average of all steps.
UX_PRD_PEAKENDRULE_001.detect: Review multi-step onboarding flows. Identify the most friction-heavy step (potential negative peak) and the final success state (end). Flag if the final step lacks clear positive reinforcement, celebration, or if stressful steps lack supportive design.
UX_PRD_PEAKENDRULE_001.when_to_apply: When designing multi-step onboarding sequences, high-stakes user actions (e.g., launching a first campaign), or complex setup flows where user anxiety might be high.
UX_PRD_PEAKENDRULE_001.when_not_to_apply: During repetitive, high-frequency utility tasks where users prioritize pure speed and efficiency over emotional engagement or 'delight'.
UX_PRD_PEAKENDRULE_001.quote: People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end, rather than the total sum or average of every moment of the experience.

UX_PRD_WIZARDPATTER_001.title: Use Wizards for Infrequent or Novice Multi-Step Tasks
UX_PRD_WIZARDPATTER_001.rule: Use a wizard pattern to guide users through complex, multi-step tasks if the process is performed infrequently (e.g., onboarding, setup) or by novice users. Avoid wizards for frequent tasks or expert users, as the step-by-step flow increases interaction cost and limits control.
UX_PRD_WIZARDPATTER_001.detect: Identify multi-step data entry flows. Check if the task is performed frequently by the same user or requires cross-referencing data across steps. If frequent or requires cross-referencing, a wizard is likely an anti-pattern.
UX_PRD_WIZARDPATTER_001.when_to_apply: When users are unfamiliar with a domain, lack expertise, or perform a complex process rarely (like initial account setup or onboarding), and need guided, sequential steps with branching logic.
UX_PRD_WIZARDPATTER_001.when_not_to_apply: When users perform the task repeatedly, need to compare information across steps, require flexible non-linear workflows, or are domain experts who need high control and efficiency.
UX_PRD_WIZARDPATTER_001.quote: Basically, use wizards for situations where the users are likely to be unfamiliar with the process — either because they don’t have a lot of domain expertise or because they go through that process only rarely.

UX_VIS_TEXTSCANNABI_001.title: Design Text for Scannability
UX_VIS_TEXTSCANNABI_001.rule: Format web text for scanning by using front-loaded and meaningful subheadings, bulleted lists, highlighted keywords, descriptive links, one idea per paragraph, and the inverted pyramid style to prevent F-pattern scanning and ensure critical content is seen.
UX_VIS_TEXTSCANNABI_001.detect: Identify dense 'walls of text' lacking structural breakers (subheadings, bulleted lists, bolded keywords), paragraphs containing multiple distinct ideas, or critical information buried in the middle or right side of text blocks.
UX_VIS_TEXTSCANNABI_001.when_to_apply: Apply to web pages, informational sites, content-heavy articles, and documentation where users are scanning for specific facts or quick answers rather than reading comprehensively.
UX_VIS_TEXTSCANNABI_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not apply to immersive reading experiences, storytelling, narrative fiction, or email newsletters where users are highly committed to reading every word and heavy formatting would disrupt the flow.
UX_VIS_TEXTSCANNABI_001.quote: People rarely read Web pages word by word; instead, they scan the page, picking out individual words and sentences.

UX_SET_IABEFORENAVI_001.title: Define Information Architecture Before Navigation UI
UX_SET_IABEFORENAVI_001.rule: Separate Information Architecture (the underlying content structure and relationships) from Navigation (the UI components used to access it). Always define the IA before selecting navigation UI patterns to ensure the UI can accommodate the full scope and depth of the content.
UX_SET_IABEFORENAVI_001.detect: Look for navigation UI patterns (e.g., inverted-L, tabs) being selected or implemented before a site map or content inventory is completed, or navigation components that artificially constrain the depth of the content.
UX_SET_IABEFORENAVI_001.when_to_apply: When designing or redesigning a website, application, or complex settings interface with multiple tiers of content and functionality.
UX_SET_IABEFORENAVI_001.when_not_to_apply: When making purely cosmetic updates to an existing UI where the underlying content structure remains completely unchanged and already fits the current navigation pattern.
UX_SET_IABEFORENAVI_001.quote: Making navigation component choices based on looks alone can force you to change an ideal IA to something that doesn’t best serve the needs of users or accommodate your content.

UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_001.title: Strictly Scope Color Tokens by CSS Property
UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_001.rule: Never mix semantic color token categories. Use background color tokens exclusively for backgrounds, text color tokens exclusively for text, and border color tokens exclusively for borders.
UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_001.detect: Analyze CSS/SCSS declarations to ensure 'color:' properties only use '$color-text-*' tokens, 'background-color:' uses '$color-background-*' tokens, and 'border-color:' uses '$color-border-*' tokens.
UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_001.when_to_apply: When applying semantic design tokens to UI components to ensure proper theming and accessibility.
UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_001.when_not_to_apply: When using primitive/global palette tokens (e.g., '$palette-blue-50') which are property-agnostic, though semantic tokens are generally preferred.
UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_001.quote: Use these tokens for background colors only. Do not use these for border colors or text colors.

UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_002.title: Standardize Medium Tap Targets at 32px
UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_002.rule: Set medium tap targets (such as standalone interactive icons) to 2rem (32px) using the designated sizing token to ensure reliable touch interaction.
UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_002.detect: Check if medium interactive icon elements utilize the '$square-icon-medium' token or explicitly set width/height to '2rem' or '32px'.
UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_002.when_to_apply: When sizing standard interactive icons and medium touch targets in a touch-friendly UI.
UX_TMP_S_TOKENS_002.when_not_to_apply: When designing high-density data interfaces that explicitly require the alternate medium tap target size (14px / 0.875rem) or smaller utility icons.

UX_TMP_EXTFIELD_001.title: Text Field Validation Timing and Error Accessibility
UX_TMP_EXTFIELD_001.rule: Validate text field input only after the user has finished interacting with the field (e.g., on blur, not during typing). Pass error messages directly to the text field's `error` prop so they are automatically linked to the input via `aria-describedby` for screen readers.
UX_TMP_EXTFIELD_001.detect: Check if validation errors trigger on every keystroke (onChange) instead of on blur. Verify that error messages are passed via the `error` prop rather than rendered as disconnected DOM nodes without `aria-describedby`.
UX_TMP_EXTFIELD_001.when_to_apply: When implementing form text fields that require validation rules and display inline error messages.
UX_TMP_EXTFIELD_001.when_not_to_apply: When providing real-time character counts, password strength meters, or auto-formatting (e.g., phone numbers), which require immediate feedback during typing.
UX_TMP_EXTFIELD_001.quote: Validate input as soon as merchants have finished interacting with a field (but not before)... When you provide help text via the helpText prop or an inline error message via the error prop, the help or error content is conveyed to screen reader users with the aria-describedby attribute.

UX_TMP_GINATION_001.title: Pagination over Infinite Scroll for Goal-Oriented Tasks
UX_TMP_GINATION_001.rule: Use pagination rather than infinite scrolling for goal-oriented finding tasks, such as locating specific content, comparing options, or backtracking. Reserve infinite scrolling for serendipitous exploration of flat-hierarchy content.
UX_TMP_GINATION_001.detect: Identify lists, search results, or feeds. Check if the loading mechanism is infinite scroll or pagination. Assess if the user's primary task is finding specific items (e.g., ecommerce) vs. open-ended browsing (e.g., social media).
UX_TMP_GINATION_001.when_to_apply: Apply pagination when users need to locate specific items, compare products, remember item locations (e.g., 'page 3'), or when accurate scrollbar representation of page length is needed.
UX_TMP_GINATION_001.when_not_to_apply: Do not use pagination when the content streams constantly, has a flat structure, and the user's goal is time-killing or serendipitous discovery.
UX_TMP_GINATION_001.quote: Endless scrolling is not recommended for goal-oriented finding tasks, such as those requiring people to locate specific content or compare options.

UX_TMP_UX_OCCAM_001.title: Occam's Razor for UI Complexity
UX_TMP_UX_OCCAM_001.rule: When evaluating competing design solutions that achieve the same goal, select the one with the fewest elements and assumptions by removing as many elements as possible without compromising function.
UX_TMP_UX_OCCAM_001.detect: Compare competing UI designs or user flows. Count the number of visual elements, required user inputs, and cognitive assumptions. Flag designs that include non-functional elements that do not contribute to the primary task.
UX_TMP_UX_OCCAM_001.when_to_apply: When refining a user interface, evaluating multiple design prototypes, or attempting to reduce cognitive load in a complex workflow.
UX_TMP_UX_OCCAM_001.when_not_to_apply: When removing elements hides critical affordances, reduces discoverability, or strips away necessary context that users need to successfully complete a task.
UX_TMP_UX_OCCAM_001.quote: Analyze each element and remove as many as possible, without compromising the overall function.

UX_TMP_VE_CARDS_001.title: Avoid Block-Wrapped Card Links
UX_TMP_VE_CARDS_001.rule: Do not wrap entire card components in an anchor tag; instead, wrap only the card's heading text in an anchor and expand its hit area using a CSS pseudo-element (::after with position: absolute).
UX_TMP_VE_CARDS_001.detect: Anchor tags (<a>) containing multiple block-level elements (headings, paragraphs, images) acting as a card container.
UX_TMP_VE_CARDS_001.when_to_apply: When building clickable teaser cards that contain a mix of images, headings, and descriptive text.
UX_TMP_VE_CARDS_001.when_not_to_apply: If the card requires multiple distinct interactive elements (e.g., author links, action buttons) that conflict with a full-card overlay, requiring a JS-based redundant click event instead.
UX_TMP_VE_CARDS_001.quote: Now, all of the card contents form the label of the link. So when a screen reader encounters it, the announcement might be something link 'Card design woes...'. It's not disastrous in terms of comprehension, but verbose — especially if the card evolves to contain more content

UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_001.title: Push Inherent Complexity to the System (Tesler's Law)
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_001.rule: Shift unavoidable process complexity away from the user and onto the system by using smart defaults, auto-complete, and structured inputs.
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_001.detect: Look for manual data entry fields (e.g., full address, university name) that could be replaced by APIs, auto-complete, or structured pickers.
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_001.when_to_apply: When collecting standardized data (addresses, dates, institutions) or when a task requires heavy cognitive load that the backend or system can automate.
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_001.when_not_to_apply: When the user needs absolute custom control over the input, or when system automation introduces high error rates.
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_001.quote: Every process has a certain amount of inherent complexity that can't be removed. You can only decide who handles it: the user or the system.

UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_002.title: Chunk Information to Respect Working Memory (Miller's Law)
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_002.rule: Group information into 5 to 9 meaningful chunks and break long forms into progressive steps of 5-7 fields to prevent cognitive overload.
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_002.detect: Identify long, unbroken lists, navigation menus with more than 9 primary items, or forms with more than 7 fields on a single page.
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_002.when_to_apply: When designing navigation menus, formatting data (like phone numbers), or building complex data-entry forms.
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_002.when_not_to_apply: When users need to scan a massive, sortable data table where pagination or chunking would hide necessary comparative context.
UX_TMP_DEMIC_UX_002.quote: The average person can hold only about 7 (+/-2) chunks of information in working memory at any given moment.

UX_TMP_M_LAYOUT_001.title: Use single-column layouts for forms
UX_TMP_M_LAYOUT_001.rule: Arrange form fields in a single column rather than multiple columns to guide user attention in a single downward direction, reducing completion time and cognitive load.
UX_TMP_M_LAYOUT_001.detect: Identify forms with fields placed side-by-side in multiple columns (excluding logical groupings like City/State/Zip).
UX_TMP_M_LAYOUT_001.when_to_apply: When designing standard data entry forms, especially on mobile devices or for checkout processes.
UX_TMP_M_LAYOUT_001.when_not_to_apply: When grouping highly related, short fields that logically belong together on a single line (e.g., City, State, and ZIP code).
UX_TMP_M_LAYOUT_001.quote: When form fields are in a single column, users' attention is guided in a single direction as users complete each field, moving down the form towards the bottom - rather than having their attention drawn both down and from side-to-side.

UX_VIS_PAGINATIONVS_001.detect: Identify lists, search results, or feeds. Check if the loading mechanism is infinite scroll or pagination. Assess if the user's primary task is finding specific items (e.g., ecommerce) vs. open-ended browsing (e.g., social media).
